raw.content:
A man in his 80s was brought to the emergency department after a cardiac arrest. According to paramedics, the patient was last seen healthy by his family 4 hours earlier, then was found unresponsive and pulseless in the bathroom. He underwent cardiopulmonary resuscitation, receiving 4 doses of epinephrine intravenously and endotracheal tube intubation with return of spontaneous circulation after approximately 10 minutes. Family later revealed he had chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) and had been complaining of shortness of breath for 2 days prior to presentation. A family member witnessed him struggling for air before losing consciousness.

Initial rhythm was pulseless electrical activity.

- ECG findings:    - Sinus rhythm at approximately 100 beats per minute    - Right axis deviation    - Prolonged QRS duration with rsR' complexes in lead V1    - Wide S waves in leads I and V6    - Prolonged r to peak R' time in lead V1    - QT interval of 360 ms measurable in leads V4-V6    - QRS duration of 133 ms in inferior leads  - Coronary angiography:    No acute occlusions found  Image Title: Figure 1. 12-Lead Electrocardiogram at Presentation  Image Title: Figure 2. Inferior and Lateral Leads From Repeated Electrocardiogram Demonstrating Discernible T Waves  Image Title: Figure 3. Leads II, III, V5, and V6 of Initial Electrocardiogram

raw.content:
A 34-year-old Thai man with a history of hypertension and tobacco use disorder, and a family history significant for polycythemia, hypertension, and stroke in his father. He initially presented with worsening bifrontal headaches, nausea, vomiting, and right-sided blurry vision. He was not adherent to his antihypertensive regimen. Three months later, he presented again with right-sided frontal headache, photophobia, tingling in his right fingers, nausea, and vomiting. He reported missing a few doses of his carvedilol and had cut down on his smoking.

Blood pressures in the emergency department ranged from 180 to 190/80-90 mm Hg during initial presentation. On second presentation, systolic blood pressures were 150 to 170 mm Hg. National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale score was 2 because of complete left homonymous hemianopsia.

- Laboratory tests: Initial presentation showed hemoglobin 20.2 g/dL, hematocrit 54.8%, MCV 74 fL, and thrombocytopenia (91,000/mm³). Second presentation showed hemoglobin 20.1 g/dL, hematocrit 57.2%, MCV 76 fL, and thrombocytopenia (76,000/mm³). Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was elevated (21 mm/h). Erythropoietin was normal (7.8 mIU/mL).- Imaging studies:  - CT Head: Left occipital intraparenchymal hemorrhage with intravascular extension (first presentation)  - CT Head: Right posterior parietal intraparenchymal hemorrhage (4.7 × 2.9 × 4.2 cm) with blood product in the right lateral ventricle and minimal midline shift (second presentation)  - MRI Brain: No underlying masses  - Peripheral smear: Showed microcytosis and thrombocytopenia without toxic granulations or blast cells- Hemoglobin Electrophoresis Results:  Hb A: 0.0%  Hb F: 1.7%  Hb A2: 4.4%  Hb E: 34.0%  Hb Tak: 59.9%

A 56-year-old man presented with a 3-month history of polyarthralgia over the bilateral wrists, knees, ankles, and left shoulder, associated with early morning stiffness and swelling of the affected joints. Once-daily celecoxib provided significant but incomplete pain relief. He noted diffuse swelling over both feet and ankles and mild puffiness of his left hand. He had no rashes, nail changes, uveitis, or constitutional symptoms. He had a 6-month duration of cough associated with occasional blood streaks, with no previous smoking history.

Synovitis was elicited over both ankles. Bilateral lower limb pitting edema up to the ankles was noted. Reduced breath sounds were heard over the right upper zone. There was no clubbing or cervical lymphadenopathy.

- Laboratory Tests:
  - Erythrocyte sedimentation rate: 40.0 mm/h
  - C-reactive protein: 41.0 mg/L
  - Rheumatoid factor: negative
  - Serum creatinine: 73.0 µmol/L (0.83 mg/dL)
  - Serum albumin: 37.0 g/L (within normal range)

- Imaging Studies:
  - Radiographs of hands, knees, ankles, and left shoulder: unremarkable for erosions
  - Chest radiograph: 8.1×6.4-cm mass in the right upper zone
  - Computed tomography of chest: lesion with paratracheal lymphadenopathy
    Image Title: Figure 1
    Image Description: Computed tomography scan of the chest demonstrating a right upper zone mass with paratracheal lymphadenopathy

- Pathology:
  - Endobronchial ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration biopsy of mediastinal lymph nodes: ALK-positive lung adenocarcinoma with mucinous features

- Additional Studies:
  - Positron emission tomography-computed tomography of full body: small foci suspicious for metastatic disease

Multicentric Castleman disease variant with TAFRO syndrome is a different lymphoproliferative disorder with distinct clinical and pathological features not supported by the vignette.

Angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma is a type of T-cell lymphoma, while the reference diagnosis is a B-cell lymphoma. The immunophenotype in the vignette (mix of small to large B lymphocytes, negative for CD5 and CD10) does not support T-cell lymphoma.
Waldenstrom macroglobulinemia is a lymphoplasmacytic lymphoma with IgM paraproteinemia, which is not indicated by the provided information.

Primary effusion lymphoma is a rare B-cell lymphoma typically associated with HHV-8 infection and presenting as effusions without a detectable tumor mass, which is not consistent with the extensive adenopathy and nodularity described.
Kaposi sarcoma is a vascular tumor caused by HHV-8, not a lymphoma, and its presentation is not consistent with the vignette.
Tuberculous pleurisy is an infectious cause of pleural effusion, while the pathology points to lymphoma. The sterile culture and specific immunophenotype rule out tuberculosis.
Chylothorax is a type of pleural effusion characterized by high triglyceride levels, which is present in the vignette. However, the underlying cause is lymphoma, not chylothorax itself.
Lymphoma is a broad category. The reference diagnosis specifies a particular type and grade of lymphoma (High-grade (3A) follicular lymphoma, stage IVB), making 'Lymphoma' too broad.
Thymoma is a tumor of the thymus gland, which is not indicated by the pathology or imaging findings, which point to widespread lymphadenopathy and pleural involvement by lymphoma.

Castleman disease is a lymphoproliferative disorder, but the specific pathological findings (mix of small to large B lymphocytes, negative for CD5 and CD10, aberrant BCL2, elevated Ki-67) are more consistent with follicular lymphoma than Castleman disease.

Nodal lymphocyte predominant Hodgkin lymphoma is a type of Hodgkin lymphoma, which is distinct from the non-Hodgkin follicular lymphoma specified in the reference diagnosis. The immunophenotype (B lymphocytes, negative for CD5 and CD10, aberrant BCL2) is not typical for Hodgkin lymphoma.
Sarcoidosis is a granulomatous inflammatory disease, not a lymphoma. The pathological findings rule out sarcoidosis.
Bronchogenic carcinoma is a type of lung cancer. While the patient has lung involvement and mediastinal density, the pathological findings of B-cell lymphoma rule out bronchogenic carcinoma.

screen_response.screen_note: The vignette describes a patient with extensive lymphadenopathy, pleural effusion, and specific pathological findings from lymph node biopsy (mix of small to large B lymphocytes, negative for CD5 and CD10, aberrant BCL2, elevated Ki-67) that are highly suggestive of a B-cell lymphoma, specifically follicular lymphoma given the BCL2 expression and B-cell lineage. The pleural fluid analysis showing high triglycerides is consistent with chylothorax, which can be caused by lymphoma.

raw.content:
A 63-year-old woman presented with difficult-to-treat hypertension. Medical history included bone and central diabetes insipidus diagnosed via femoral biopsy 12 years ago, and liver involvement three years prior that was treated with cytarabine for one year. The patient had untreated dyslipidemia (LDL cholesterol 3.11 mmol/L). She was not a smoker and did not have diabetes. Her body mass index was 19.22 kg/m². No relevant family history was reported. The patient did not report angina, exertional dyspnea, or claudication.

Blood pressure was 198/106 mmHg without orthostatic hypotension or anisosphygmia, and heart rate was 65 beats/min. The cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable, and a continuous murmur was heard in the epigastric region.

- Laboratory Tests:    * Serum creatinine: 96.36 μmol/L (1.09 mg/dL)    * Potassium: 4.4 mmol/L    * B-type natriuretic peptide: 82,500 pg/mL    * Inflammatory markers: normal    * Urinalysis: unremarkable without albuminuria  - Imaging Studies:    * Transthoracic echocardiogram: left ventricular mass index of 110 g/m² without other relevant changes    * Abdominal CT angiogram:      Title: Contrast-enhanced abdominal CT      Description: Right kidney atrophy without discernible right renal artery and high-grade ostial stenosis of the left renal, celiac trunk, and superior mesenteric arteries    * Diethylenetriamine pentaacetate renogram: confirmed right kidney functional exclusion    * Renal vein catheterization: no signs of renin production lateralization

semantic_screen.reference_diagnosis: Recurrent plaque erosion presenting as Non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI)

candidate_relations.reason: Myocardial bridging is a congenital anomaly where a segment of a coronary artery runs intramyocardially, which is not indicated by the findings of a filling defect and elevated troponin. The reference diagnosis is about plaque erosion and NSTEMI.

The reference diagnosis specifies 'Non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI)', which is a type of acute myocardial infarction. The candidate is a broader but clinically acceptable term given the context of elevated troponin and chest pain.

Coronary artery thrombosis is the underlying mechanism for the 'filling defect' and the NSTEMI, but it is not the primary diagnosis of 'plaque erosion presenting as NSTEMI'. It's a component of the pathophysiology rather than the full diagnosis.

Vasculitis is inflammation of blood vessels. While it can affect coronary arteries, there is no evidence in the vignette to suggest vasculitis as the cause of the filling defect or NSTEMI. The reference diagnosis points to plaque erosion.

Takayasu arteritis is a specific type of large vessel vasculitis, primarily affecting the aorta and its major branches. There is no clinical or imaging evidence to support this diagnosis in the vignette. The reference diagnosis is plaque erosion and NSTEMI.

Coronary artery embolism is a cause of acute coronary syndrome, but the vignette describes a 'filling defect' and 'plaque erosion' as the underlying cause, not an embolus originating from elsewhere. While an embolus can cause a filling defect, the specific etiology in the reference diagnosis is plaque erosion.

Intracoronary thrombus is the direct cause of the 'filling defect' and the NSTEMI in this case, resulting from plaque erosion. However, the reference diagnosis specifies the underlying pathology of 'plaque erosion presenting as NSTEMI', making intracoronary thrombus a component rather than the full diagnosis.

Giant cell arteritis is a systemic vasculitis primarily affecting large and medium-sized arteries, typically in older adults. There is no evidence in the vignette to suggest this diagnosis. The reference diagnosis is plaque erosion and NSTEMI.

Kawasaki disease is an acute vasculitis primarily affecting children, leading to coronary artery aneurysms. This patient is a 39-year-old man, and there is no evidence of Kawasaki disease. The reference diagnosis is plaque erosion and NSTEMI.

Spontaneous coronary artery dissection (SCAD) involves a tear in the coronary artery wall. While it can cause NSTEMI, the OCT findings in the vignette describe a 'filling defect' and 'plaque erosion', not a dissection. The reference diagnosis is plaque erosion and NSTEMI.

Thromboangiitis obliterans (Buerger's disease) is a rare inflammatory disease of small and medium-sized arteries and veins, typically affecting the limbs of smokers. There is no evidence in the vignette to suggest this diagnosis. The reference diagnosis is plaque erosion and NSTEMI.

screen_response.screen_note: The reference diagnosis specifies 'Recurrent plaque erosion presenting as Non-ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (NSTEMI)'. The candidate 'Acute myocardial infarction' is a broader category that encompasses NSTEMI, making it an acceptable clinical variant. Other candidates like 'Coronary artery thrombosis' and 'Intracoronary thrombus' describe the immediate pathological event but not the underlying cause (plaque erosion) or the full clinical syndrome (NSTEMI).

vignette:
A 65-year-old man with a history of hepatitis B, hepatitis C, rheumatoid arthritis, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease, hypertension, hyperlipidemia, and obesity presented with several months of facial swelling, dysphagia, and dysarthria. Shortly thereafter, he developed a pruritic rash on his trunk and upper extremities. He did not report a personal or family history of angioedema. His medications included lisinopril, atorvastatin, albuterol, and ibuprofen for rheumatoid arthritis. The patient had discontinued etanercept six months before presentation. He presented to the emergency department two weeks after seeing his primary care provider for a persistent periorbital, chest, and upper extremity rash. His rash worsened, and he noted new throat swelling and weakness.

Vital signs were stable on arrival. Physical examination was notable for anasarca and a diffuse coalescent erythematous rash over the extremities, chest, and abdomen, with scaling and crusting of the back. There was a heliotrope rash and erythematous lip swelling. He had weakness to resistance in all extremities and a muffled voice without tongue swelling. Over several days, the patient's shoulder and hip weakness progressed, and he could not lift his arms above his head or stand without assistance.

On the 12th day after second vaccination, he developed fever. Initial symptoms gradually worsened leading to hospitalization on the 24th day after second vaccination. After initial discharge, he was readmitted for chest pain.

Initial presentation included fever and erythema on the trunk and extremities. During readmission, patient presented with chest pain that was refractory and persistent.

Laboratory Tests (Initial admission):- C-reactive protein: 19.77 mg/dL (normal, <0.15 mg/dL)- Leukocyte count: 12,480/μL (normal, 3,500−9,700/μL)- Platelet count: 271 × 10³/μL (normal, 140−379 × 10³/μL)- Serum ferritin: 443.1 ng/mL (normal, 21−282 ng/mL)- D-dimer: 1.1 µg/mL (normal, <1.0 µg/mL)Laboratory Tests (Readmission):- High-sensitivity troponin I: 6327 pg/mL (normal, <26.2 pg/mL)- Creatine phosphokinase: 325 U/L (normal, 38−196 U/L)- D-dimer: 1.6 µg/mL- Platelet count: 87 × 10³/μLImaging Studies:1. Initial contrast-enhanced CT:- Revealed hepatosplenomegaly- Contrast-enhanced defective area in kidney2. Coronary angiography:- Total occlusion of atrioventricular branch of right coronary artery- 90% stenotic lesions with >3 mm coronary ectasia in left circumflex artery3. Optical coherence tomography:- Showed blurring of intravascular structure- Intimal thickening- Medial vessel destruction- Thrombi in RCA and LCx lesions4. Follow-up contrast-enhanced CT:- New intrahepatic arterial luminal irregularities- Enlarged contrast-enhanced defective area in kidneySARS-CoV-2 PCR test results were repeatedly negative

candidate_relations.reason: The testicular ultrasound was negative for neoplasm, ruling out testicular cancer as the primary site. While there is a retroperitoneal mass, the primary is adrenal choriocarcinoma, not testicular cancer with retroperitoneal metastasis.

The pathology results clearly indicate a choriocarcinoma, not a sarcoma. Immunostaining for AE1/AE3, CAM5.2, inhibin, β-hCG, Glypican-3, and PLAP are consistent with choriocarcinoma, while negative for markers typically associated with sarcoma.

The pathology results are inconsistent with adrenal cortical carcinoma. Immunostaining for β-hCG (strongly positive) and Glypican-3 (focally positive) are characteristic of choriocarcinoma, not adrenal cortical carcinoma. Also, the normal cortisol and ACTH levels argue against adrenal cortical carcinoma.

This is too broad. While there is metastatic disease (pulmonary nodules) and a retroperitoneal mass, the specific primary diagnosis is adrenal choriocarcinoma with pulmonary metastases, which is more precise than just 'metastatic disease to the retroperitoneum.'

While the initial CT described a 'hemorrhagic mass-like density,' the subsequent MRI and pathology confirmed a tumor (choriocarcinoma), not just a hemorrhage. The hemorrhage was a feature of the tumor, not the primary diagnosis itself.
This is too broad. Choriocarcinoma is a type of germ cell tumor, but the reference diagnosis specifies the exact type and location (Primary Adrenal Choriocarcinoma).

The reference diagnosis is 'Primary Adrenal Choriocarcinoma with pulmonary metastases'. An extragonadal germ cell tumor, specifically choriocarcinoma, originating in the adrenal gland, is an acceptable clinical variant. The testicular ultrasound was negative, confirming an extragonadal origin.
This is too broad. While the tumor is a choriocarcinoma, the reference diagnosis specifies the primary location (adrenal) and the presence of metastases (pulmonary).

The pathology results are inconsistent with lymphoma. Immunostaining for AE1/AE3, CAM5.2, inhibin, β-hCG, Glypican-3, and PLAP are characteristic of choriocarcinoma, while negative for CD30, which can be positive in some lymphomas, but the overall profile does not support lymphoma.

While there was an adrenal mass and elevated metanephrines, the pathology results (strongly positive β-hCG, specific trophoblastic cell types) definitively rule out pheochromocytoma and confirm choriocarcinoma. The elevated metanephrines could be a paraneoplastic phenomenon or a co-occurrence, but not the primary diagnosis.

raw.content:
An 81-year-old man initially developed a cough, subjective fever, and shortness of breath. He was first treated with azithromycin for bronchitis, followed by levofloxacin after a right upper lobe infiltrate was found. His symptoms progressed despite antibiotics. Medical history includes coronary artery disease with coronary artery bypass (two years prior), atrial fibrillation on rivaroxaban, heart failure with reduced ejection fraction, stage 3 chronic kidney disease, and type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c: 8.1%). He had spent time at a Northern Minnesota cabin but reported minimal outdoor exposure. Previous missionary work in Colombia ended two years before admission. Never smoked and rarely consumed alcohol.

Vital signs: Temperature 38.6°C, Pulse 130 beats/min, Blood Pressure 114/61 mm Hg, Respiratory Rate 22 breaths/min, Oxygen Saturation 82% (improved to >90% with 5 L/min oxygen). Lung sounds were diminished in the right upper lobe, with diffuse crackles in the right lung base. No clubbing or cyanosis. Cardiac examination showed tachycardic irregularly irregular rhythm, systolic ejection murmur, and mild pitting edema to the knee bilaterally. No cervical or axillary lymphadenopathy. Neurologic and skin examinations were normal. Later developed right-sided ptosis and anisocoria with an asymmetrically miotic right pupil (more evident in dark environment).

Laboratory Tests:
- Leukocytosis: 15,000/mm³
- Procalcitonin: 0.77 ng/mL
- Positive Blastomyces urine antigen
- Positive Histoplasmosis blood antigen
- Negative results for Mycobacterium tuberculosis
- Negative antigen tests for Cryptococcus, Legionella, and influenza
- Negative Paracoccidioides serum antibody

candidate_relations.reason: Hemophagocytic Lymphohistiocytosis (HLH) is a more general term for the hemophagocytosis described in the reference diagnosis. The reference diagnosis specifies 'hemophagocytosis' as a complication, which is a key feature of HLH. While the reference diagnosis is more specific about the underlying cause (Kikuchi-Fujimoto disease), HLH is an acceptable clinical variant for the hemophagocytic component.

Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) can cause fever, lymphadenopathy, and positive ANA, but the specific histopathology of necrotizing lymphadenitis with apoptotic bodies and hemophagocytosis, along with negative ENA/APL/ANCA, points away from SLE as the primary diagnosis.

Herpes Simplex Encephalitis typically presents with focal neurological deficits, seizures, and characteristic MRI findings (temporal lobe involvement), which are not fully consistent with the diffuse leptomeningeal thickening and the overall clinical picture dominated by lymphadenopathy and systemic inflammation.
Cytomegalovirus Encephalitis is less likely given the specific lymph node pathology and the absence of other typical CMV manifestations in an immunocompetent individual.

Infectious Mononucleosis can cause fever, lymphadenopathy, and splenomegaly, but the specific histopathology of necrotizing lymphadenitis with apoptotic bodies and hemophagocytosis is not typical for infectious mononucleosis. The CSF findings are also more severe than usually seen in uncomplicated mononucleosis.

Lymphomatoid Granulomatosis is a rare lymphoproliferative disorder that typically affects the lungs, skin, and central nervous system, but the specific histopathology described (necrotizing lymphadenitis with apoptotic bodies and hemophagocytosis) is not characteristic of lymphomatoid granulomatosis.

Juvenile Rheumatoid Arthritis (now Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis) is a chronic inflammatory arthritis, and while it can cause systemic symptoms, the specific lymph node pathology and severe CSF findings are not typical for JRA.

Tuberculous Meningitis can cause fever, headache, meningeal irritation, and CSF abnormalities (high protein, mononuclear pleocytosis), but the specific lymph node histopathology (necrotizing lymphadenitis with apoptotic bodies and hemophagocytosis) and the absence of granulomas or acid-fast bacilli are not consistent with TB.

Kikuchi-Fujimoto Disease (KFD) is explicitly mentioned as the primary diagnosis in the reference, and the clinical and pathological findings (fever, lymphadenopathy, necrotizing lymphadenitis with apoptotic bodies, histiocytes, and hemophagocytosis) are highly characteristic of KFD.

Subacute Sclerosing Panencephalitis is a rare, chronic, progressive encephalitis caused by measles virus, typically presenting with cognitive decline, myoclonus, and seizures, which is not consistent with the acute presentation and specific lymph node pathology in this case.
Histiocytic Necrotizing Lymphadenitis is an alternative name for Kikuchi-Fujimoto Disease, which is the primary diagnosis in the reference.

A 56-year-old male presented with right lower abdominal pain, nausea, and vomiting for one month. The vomitus included stomach contents and bile. He had undergone bariatric surgery 10 years prior. His weight history showed: preoperative weight 127 kg, decreased to 95 kg three months post-surgery, increased to 118 kg five months ago due to changed eating habits, and recently lost 23 kg due to poor appetite and abdominal pain.

Physical findings included:- Localized tenderness and rebound pain in the right lower abdomen- No obvious muscle tension- Active bowel sounds- Sound of gas passing through water could be heard- Vital signs were stable

Laboratory Tests:- White blood cells: 15.3 × 109- Neutrophils: 13.25 × 109- C-reactive protein: 190 mg/L- Albumin: 24 g/L- Normal renal function and coagulation testsImaging Studies:1. Plain Abdominal Radiography:- Free gas under the right diaphragm- Dilated upper jejunum with 'spring sign'2. Abdominal CT:- Scattered pneumatosis in abdominal cavity- Thickened intestinal wall- Dense tubular shadows in narrow lumen3. A 13-year-old boy presented with a five-day history of left scrotal soreness and oedema. The patient had no lower urinary tract symptoms and no major relevant medical or surgical history. Based on penile characteristics, the patient was diagnosed with occult penis. Other congenital anomalies of the genitourinary tract were excluded based on imaging findings.

Scrotal investigation revealed an enlarged testis, epididymis, and infected appendages. No torsion was evident in the sperm vessels; however, purulent foci were visible on the surface of the vessels, and their texture was tough and inseparable. The patient was at Tanner stage G4P4.

- Laboratory tests: Blood workup showed mild leukocytosis (18.5 × 109/L). Urine analysis was negative. Pus culture isolated P. aeruginosa, susceptible to ceftazidime and ofloxacin.- Imaging studies:  1. Doppler ultrasonography: Revealed an enlarged left testis with heterogeneous echo pattern, enhanced vascularity, and retained testicular blood flow.  2. Follow-up sonography: Showed heterogeneous echotexture in the left testis and epididymis, with a mild whirlpool sign and hyperechogenicity in the inguinal area.  3. MRI Image (at 60 days):     Title: MR imaging of testes     Description: Left testis showed no enhancement in T2, indicating disappearance of the left testis.- Pathological examination: Showed hemorrhagic infarction of the left testicular appendage and fibrocystic-like tissue with inflammatory cell infiltration.

Prenatal ultrasound showed slightly enhanced parenchymal echoes and enlarged kidneys bilaterally. A 39-year-old male patient was admitted to hospital with recurrent post-activity chest pain and shortness of breath for more than 11 years and bilateral lower extremity edema for one week in March 2021. His symptoms began in 2010 when he first experienced post-activity chest pain and shortness of breath for half a year. The patient was initially acyanotic from 2010 to 2016, but gradually became cyanotic after an episode of severe cough and hemoptysis (approximately 50ml in volume) following a severe cold leading to pneumonia in July 2016.

The patient presented with mild bilateral lower extremity edema. Femoral artery oxygen saturation was measured at 88.5% (decreased from a previous measurement of 93.4% in 2016).

A 62-year-old male patient presented with cough and sputum with intermittent fever for 3 days. Past medical history included tuberculosis 10 years ago which was cured after systematic anti-tuberculosis treatment. gold: Intra-atrial reentrant tachycardia (IART) with variable atrioventricular block

semantic_screen.reference_diagnosis: Intra-atrial reentrant tachycardia (IART) with variable atrioventricular block

candidate_relations.reason: Supraventricular tachycardia is a broader category that includes IART, but it lacks the specificity of the reference diagnosis.

Intra-atrial reentrant tachycardia is the core diagnosis. The 'with variable atrioventricular block' is a descriptive finding rather than a distinct diagnosis, and its omission does not change the primary diagnosis.
Wolf-Parkinson-White syndrome is a pre-excitation syndrome involving an accessory pathway, which is not indicated in the vignette.

Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT) is a type of supraventricular tachycardia, but the ECG findings (visible P waves in lead V1 and lead II, grouped beating, and continuation of SVT after adenosine with temporary heart block) are more consistent with an atrial tachycardia like IART rather than AVNRT.
Permanent junctional reciprocating tachycardia (PJRT) is a type of AVRT, but the ECG findings are more suggestive of an atrial reentrant tachycardia rather than a junctional one.

Ectopic atrial tachycardia is a type of atrial tachycardia, but the description of reentrant tachycardia is more specific and supported by the context of congenital heart disease and prior surgery, which predisposes to reentrant circuits.
Orthodromic atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia (AVRT) involves an accessory pathway, which is not indicated. The ECG findings are more consistent with an intra-atrial reentrant mechanism.

Atrial flutter is a type of macro-reentrant atrial tachycardia, but the ECG description of 'irregularly irregular tachycardia with grouped beating and intermittently visible P waves' and 'regular narrow complex tachycardia with visible P waves' after diltiazem, followed by SVT continuation after adenosine, is more consistent with IART rather than typical atrial flutter with its characteristic sawtooth waves.

Focal atrial tachycardia is a type of atrial tachycardia originating from a single focus, but the clinical context of complex congenital heart disease and Fontan circulation strongly suggests a reentrant mechanism, making IART a more likely diagnosis.

Atrial fibrillation is characterized by chaotic atrial activity and irregularly irregular ventricular response without organized P waves, which is not fully consistent with the ECG descriptions provided, especially the presence of visible P waves and grouped beating.

screen_response.screen_note: The reference diagnosis includes a descriptive finding ('with variable atrioventricular block') which is not a separate diagnosis. The core diagnosis is Intra-atrial reentrant tachycardia.

gold: Trifascicular heart block (Bifascicular block with first-degree AV block progressing to complete heart block)

semantic_screen.reference_diagnosis: Trifascicular heart block (Bifascicular block with first-degree AV block progressing to complete heart block)

candidate_relations.reason: The vignette describes a patient with trifascicular heart block, not arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy. There is no mention of structural abnormalities of the right ventricle or ventricular arrhythmias characteristic of ARVC.

Sick sinus syndrome involves dysfunction of the sinus node, leading to bradycardia or alternating bradycardia/tachycardia. While the patient has bradycardia and AV block, the primary issue is conduction system disease (trifascicular block) rather than sinus node dysfunction. The 24-hour ECG shows sinus rhythm with AV block, not sick sinus syndrome.

Vasovagal syncope is a reflex syncope, typically triggered by specific situations and not associated with the severe conduction abnormalities (trifascicular block progressing to complete heart block) seen in this patient.

The patient has pulmonary hypertension, but the primary diagnosis is trifascicular heart block, which is the cause of the syncope and dyspnea. There is no information to suggest idiopathic pulmonary arterial hypertension as the primary diagnosis, and the pulmonary hypertension could be secondary to other cardiac issues or age-related changes.

Dilated cardiomyopathy is characterized by left ventricular dilation and systolic dysfunction. The patient's echocardiogram shows normal left ventricular ejection fraction (74%) and normal wall motion, ruling out dilated cardiomyopathy.
Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is characterized by left ventricular hypertrophy. The vignette does not mention any left ventricular hypertrophy, and the primary issue is conduction system disease.
Mitral stenosis is a valvular heart disease. The echocardiogram explicitly states 'No significant valvular abnormality'.
Aortic stenosis is a valvular heart disease. The echocardiogram explicitly states 'No significant valvular abnormality'.

Restrictive cardiomyopathy is characterized by impaired ventricular filling due to rigid ventricular walls. The echocardiogram does not suggest restrictive cardiomyopathy; it shows normal LVEF and normal wall motion, with uncertain diastolic function, but no clear evidence of restriction.

Atrioventricular nodal reentrant tachycardia (AVNRT) is a type of supraventricular tachycardia. The patient's ECGs show various degrees of AV block and bradycardia, not AVNRT. The 24-hour ECG specifically states 'No atrial/ventricular arrhythmia found'.

Pulmonary embolism is a blockage in one of the pulmonary arteries in the lungs. While the patient has dyspnea and pulmonary hypertension, there are no other signs or symptoms suggestive of acute pulmonary embolism, and the primary issue is the severe conduction system disease.

Cardiac amyloidosis is a restrictive cardiomyopathy caused by amyloid deposition in the heart. There is no evidence in the vignette to suggest cardiac amyloidosis; the echocardiogram does not show typical findings, and the primary problem is electrical conduction disease.

screen_response.screen_note: The patient's symptoms of syncope and dyspnea on exertion, along with the ECG findings of first-degree AV block, RBBB, LAFB (constituting trifascicular block), and progression to Mobitz type I second-degree AV block and third-degree AV block, strongly point to a severe cardiac conduction disorder as the primary diagnosis. The other conditions are either ruled out by clinical or echocardiographic findings or are not the most likely primary diagnosis explaining the syncope and severe conduction abnormalities.

vignette:
A patient in their 80s presented with dyspnea and syncope during exercise. Medical history included essential hypertension and Parkinson disease. The patient reported experiencing dyspnea on exertion and exercise intolerance for the past year, with difficulty walking more than 100m. They also experienced syncope during a bicycle ride with loss of consciousness for a few minutes, followed by complete recovery.

raw.content:
A man in his 50s presented with an asymptomatic, arc-shaped, depressed skin groove on the left side of his forehead, frontal scalp, and vertex area. Localized linear hair loss and hair thinning on the left scalp area were observed. The patient reported that when the lesion had begun approximately 10 years earlier, he had received 2 doses of intralesional steroid via injection on a small bald patch on the vertex. Thereafter, the lesion gradually progressed to the frontal scalp and eventually made a linear furrow on the left side of his forehead. The patient denied any trauma history and had no history of connective tissue disease nor any evidence of systemic involvement, such as arthralgia, photosensitivity, or skin rashes.

Examination revealed 2 long, curved-line, depressed, alopecic patches on the left side of the vertex and frontal scalp area extending to the left eyebrow. The lesions measured (length × width) 7 × 2 cm and 6 × 1 cm, respectively. Dermoscopic examination of the alopecic area revealed several short vellus hairs, yellow dots, and honeycomb hyperpigmentation; however, broken hairs were not seen. The result of a hair pull test was negative.

- Histopathologic examination:    Image A: Clinical image of annular arc from a longitudinally furrowed skin lesion on the left eyebrow and forehead to an alopecic lesion    Image B: Clinical image of the bandlike grooved alopecic lesion on the left side of the frontal scalp and vertex    Image C: Scanning view shows predominant lymphocytic infiltrates in perifollicular and periappendageal regions of the dermis and lobular panniculitis (hematoxylin-eosin staining)    Image D: High-power view shows inflammatory infiltrates between adipocytes with hyaline fat necrosis in the subcutis (hematoxylin-eosin staining)  - Laboratory findings:    - Direct immunofluorescence: Positive with granular deposition of IgG, IgA, IgM, C3, C1q, and fibrinogen in the dermal blood vessels    - Antinuclear antibody: Negative    - Antidouble-stranded DNA antibody: Negative    - All other laboratory test findings were normal

raw.content:
A woman in her 40s presented with blurred vision in the right eye. She was undergoing treatment with systemic steroids, durvalumab (a PD-L1 inhibitor), and bevacizumab. Ten days after initial presentation, the patient developed sudden vision loss in the right eye.

Initial examination: Visual acuity of 20/25 OU. Right eye showed full visual field, right-sided relative afferent pupillary defect, unremarkable anterior segment, and mild swelling of the optic disc. Left eye had normal fundus and visual function. Follow-up examination (after vision loss): Right eye showed no light perception vision, marked swelling of the optic disc, peripapillary retinal hemorrhages, and occlusion of the superior branch artery. Two days later: Combined occlusion of the central retinal artery and vein, and a new collection of whitish material suspended anterior to the optic disc, forming a pocket in the posterior vitreous.

- Imaging Studies:    Image Title: MRI at Onset of Vision Loss    Image Description:     - Coronal T1-weighted contrast-enhanced image: Focal enhancement along enlarged right optic nerve    - Axial T1-weighted contrast-enhanced image: Diffuse enlargement of orbital portion of right optic nerve, enhancement of nerve sheath, slight flattening of posterior globe    - Coronal T2-weighted (FLAIR) image: Hyperintensity of right optic nerve  - Laboratory Tests:    - Lumbar puncture showed no abnormalities      - Other Tests:    - Wide-field fluorescein angiography: Showed choroidal flush but complete lack of perfusion of retinal vasculature      - Pathological Examination:    - Vitreous biopsy: Hypercellular sample with astrocytic neoplasm, small to medium-sized cells with scant cytoplasm and oval, pleomorphic, hyperchromatic nuclei    - Immunohistochemistry: Positive for glial fibrillary acid protein, oligodendrocyte transcription factor 2, mutant IDH-1 protein, p53; Loss of ATRX protein; Ki-67 proliferation index ~10%

raw.content:
A man in his 70s presented with swelling of the manubrium 12 years after resection of a large left substernal thyroid lobe through a midline sternotomy approach. The swelling was slightly tender and had increased in size markedly over the month prior to presentation. Medical history includes previous substernal left hemithyroidectomy for benign goiter 12 years ago.

Swelling noted over the manubrium, which was slightly tender.

- Imaging Studies:    CT Image Title: Computed Tomographic Image Demonstrating Lytic Mass of Manubrium    CT Image Description: Shows a lytic lesion replacing the manubrium measuring 2.7 × 4.4 × 5.8 cm and residual right goiter. The posterior aspect is in close proximity to the brachiocephalic artery and the left innominate vein.    - Fine-needle aspiration:    Revealed follicular thyroid cells in the goiter and the manubrial lesion.    - Pathological Examination:    Image Title: Thyroid Follicles With Nuclear Features Infiltrating Adjacent to Bone Trabeculae    Image Description: Hematoxylin-eosin stained specimens showing thyroid follicles infiltrating adjacent to bone trabeculae (at ×20 and ×10 magnification).

vignette:
An obese man in his mid-30s with no prior systemic or ocular disorders presented to a local emergency department after waking with vision loss in his right eye. The night prior, he had been drinking alcohol heavily and took 2 buprenorphine hydrochloride/naloxone hydrochloride pills. He denied any trauma. He also experienced pain, numbness, and erythematous induration of his right eyelids and forearm that increased throughout the day.

Visual acuity: No light perception in right eye (OD) and 20/20 in left eye (OS). Right eye showed tense eyelid edema, chemosis, corneal haze, and restricted motility in all fields of gaze. Right pupil was mid-dilated with a relative afferent pupillary defect. Intraocular pressure was 37 mm Hg OD and 21 mm Hg OS. Ophthalmoscopic examination revealed tortuous vessels, serous retinal detachment sparing the inferior periphery, and macular whitening. Left eye examination was normal.

- Laboratory Tests:
Creatinine level: 2.2 mg/dL
Creatine kinase level: 29,320 U/L

- Imaging Studies:
1. Noncontrast computed tomography of head and orbits: Showed periorbital soft-tissue swelling

2. Optical Coherence Tomography:
Image Title: OCT of the Right Eye
Image Description: Demonstrates severe disorganization of the retinal architecture, subretinal fluid, and sub-retinal pigment epithelial fluid

3. Fluorescein Angiography:
Image Title: Fluorescein Angiography of the Right Eye
Image Description: Shows delayed choroidal filling, delayed retinal arterial filling, patchy temporal hyperfluorescence, diffuse leakage and poor vascular perfusion in various phases

raw.content:
A woman in her 50s presented with 4 days of blurry vision and pain in her left eye after undergoing a routine dental cleaning 1 week prior. She had no history of gingival disease or cavities. Her medical and ocular histories were unremarkable.

Visual acuity was 20/25 OD and 20/50 OS. Intraocular pressures were 15 mm Hg OD and 11 mm Hg OS. Left eye examination showed conjunctival hyperemia, faint keratic precipitates, 3+ cells with fibrin in the anterior chamber, mild nuclear sclerosis, and a whitish focal granuloma at the 4-o'clock position at the pupillary margin. The posterior segment was unremarkable, with no evidence of vitritis, retinitis, or vasculitis. The right eye was unremarkable. At 1-day follow-up, visual acuity declined to 20/100 OS, with development of hypopyon and increased fibrinous material emanating from the iris lesion. No posterior segment involvement was noted.

- Microscopy: Gram stain revealed gram-positive cocci in chains and gram-positive rods in a branching pattern.  Image Title: Gram Stain of Iris Abscess  Image Description: Mixed flora of gram-positive cocci in pairs and chains and gram-positive bacilli (original magnification ×400)- Cultures: Aerobic culture revealed Streptococcus intermedius. The gram-positive bacilli could not be identified more specifically.- Additional Tests: Blood and urine cultures, electrocardiogram and echocardiogram were unremarkable.

A 13-year-old boy presented with an intensely pruritic skin eruption that appeared approximately 24 hours after intensive sun exposure in spring. The patient was otherwise healthy but reported an episode of malaise and headache 2 weeks before first presentation. He had no history of photosensitivity, and denied the use of any topical or systemic photosensitizers.

PVB19 DNA was found (viral load of 0.2 PVB19 DNA copies/β-globin gene copy, or 33,438 copies/μg of isolated DNA) in lesional skin biopsy specimen, but not in the serum.- Other tests: Standard phototesting with UV-A and UV-B was unremarkable.- Images:  Image 1 Title: The Patient's Clinical Findings on the Ears at First Presentation  Image 1 Description: Helical thickening, erythema, and numerous small vesicles are present on both ears  Image 2 Title: The Patient's Facial Lesions  Image 2 Description: Crusted papules and small erosions are located on the cheeks. Several blisters are located at the upper and lower vermillion border

raw.content:
A 65-year-old woman presented with blurry vision in her right eye for several months. Ocular history included 3 recurrent episodes of bilateral iritis occurring during 5 months, amblyopia in the left eye, and bilateral posterior chamber intraocular lens. Patient had undergone left-sided mastectomy 2.5 years prior and had been on anastrozole therapy for more than 2 years. Medical history and past medication use were otherwise unremarkable.

Visual acuity: 20/25 OD and 20/150 OS without improvement on pinhole testing. Intraocular pressures were normal. Right eye showed trace conjunctival injection without definite ciliary flush, 2+ fine keratic precipitates, and 1+ cells in the anterior chamber. Left eye had a few keratic precipitates. Dilated fundus examination revealed cystoid macular edema with a yellow spot in the fovea in the right eye and an epiretinal membrane in the left eye. No inflammation in the periphery was noted in either eye.

- Optical Coherence Tomography (OCT):  Image Title: OCT Scans  Image Description: Right eye showed significant cystoid macular edema and subfoveal fluid. Left eye had a mild epiretinal membrane.- Fluorescein Angiography:  Image Title: Fundus Fluorescein Angiography  Image Description: Revealed cystoid macular edema with leakage in both right and left eyes.- Blood Tests: Tests for vasculitis and rheumatologic disorders were within reference limits. Normal findings for tick-borne and bacterial diseases.- Imaging:  Computed tomography of the chest was unremarkable.

raw.content:
A 36-year-old man with end-stage renal disease secondary to IgA nephropathy underwent a live-related renal transplant 6 months ago and has been maintained on tacrolimus 3.5 mg daily, mycophenolate sodium 720 mg daily, and prednisolone 7.5 mg daily. He presented with a 14-day history of low-grade fever, dry cough, and anorexia without dyspnea, chest pain, hemoptysis, or weight loss. He was afebrile on admission, heart rate 88 beats/min, blood pressure 122/76 mm Hg, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. Examination revealed bilateral inspiratory crackles; other findings were unremarkable.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL; total lymphocyte count 9900/μL; absolute neutrophil count 7720/μL; platelets 285 000/μL; serum creatinine 1.05 mg/dL. Arterial blood gas analysis demonstrated PaO₂ 68 mm Hg and an A–a gradient of 22 mm Hg. HIV ELISA was negative. Chest radiograph revealed bilateral diffuse alveolar infiltrates. High-resolution CT of the chest showed bilateral diffuse ground-glass opacities without pleural or mediastinal abnormalities.

Sputum induction was non-diagnostic. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) fluid was positive for Pneumocystis jirovecii on Grocott’s methenamine silver stain and negative for acid-fast bacilli, CMV inclusion bodies, and fungal hyphae. He was treated with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole and a prednisone taper, with clinical and radiographic resolution of infiltrates after 2 weeks.

Three weeks into therapy, he was asymptomatic except for an occasional dry cough. TMP-SMX was discontinued, and prednisolone was maintained at 10 mg daily. Laboratory studies then showed leukopenia (TLC 1400/μL; ANC 1050/μL). Chest radiograph revealed new left upper-zone infiltrates. Repeat HRCT showed resolution of ground-glass opacities and new patchy peribronchovascular consolidations in the right upper lobe, left upper lobe, and left lower-lobe apical segment. Repeat BAL was negative for AFB, fungus, and Pneumocystis jirovecii. 

Transbronchial lung biopsy from the left upper lobe showed alveoli filled with inflammatory debris consisting of granulation tissue, interstitial inflammation, and areas of intra-alveolar fibrin deposition.

A 9-year-old girl with a small muscular ventricular septal defect presented with chest pain and dyspnea one week after recovering from an upper respiratory infection and after minor anterior chest trauma in a fall. She was afebrile. Heart rate was 104 beats/min, respiratory rate 28 breaths/min, blood pressure 113/66 mm Hg, and oxygen saturation normal. Physical examination revealed mild tenderness over the sternum and normal cardiac auscultation. 

Chest radiography showed mild cardiomediastinal silhouette enlargement and a focal opacity in the right middle lung. ECG was normal. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated a moderate circumferential pericardial effusion with right atrial collapse, normal biventricular systolic function, and no ventricular septal defect. 

Laboratory studies revealed a leukocyte count of 12,000 cells/µL with an absolute eosinophil count of 1,570 cells/µL (normal 40–190), C-reactive protein 1.94 mg/dL (normal <0.5), erythrocyte sedimentation rate 45 mm/hr (normal 0–30), and troponin T 0.25 ng/mL (normal <0.1). Cardiac magnetic resonance imaging showed elevated global myocardial T2 (70 ms) and T1 (1150 ms) values, increased left ventricular wall thickness, a moderate pericardial effusion, and no late gadolinium enhancement.

She was admitted with a working diagnosis of viral myopericarditis. Treatment with oral ibuprofen and colchicine resulted in resolution of chest pain, normalization of troponin and inflammatory markers, and reduction of the pericardial effusion over three days. However, the absolute eosinophil count rose further. Consultations with infectious diseases, allergy/immunology, and rheumatology were obtained. Further history elicited pica and exposure to two dogs and a cat. 

Chest computed tomography revealed multiple pulmonary nodules with adjacent ground-glass opacities. An infectious workup showed negative PCR tests for influenza, respiratory syncytial virus, parainfluenza virus, rhinovirus, and adenovirus; negative Bartonella henselae titers; and a negative T-SPOT tuberculosis test. raw.content:
A 53-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and bipolar disorder was admitted for a 4-week history of progressive asthenia, anorexia, and a 7-kg weight loss, with vomiting during the last 2 days. On examination, her BMI was 18.2 kg/m2 and she was obnubilated; the ECG was normal. Laboratory studies showed:  
• Serum calcium 3.8 mmol/L (normal phosphorus), nonregenerative normocytic normochromic anemia (hemoglobin 9 g/dL), and acute functional renal failure (creatinine clearance 30 mL/min).  
• PTH 9 ng/L.  
• Polyclonal hypergammaglobulinemia; negative 24-hour proteinuria; no monoclonal peak on serum or urine immunoelectrophoresis; normal serum free light-chain ratio.  

She received IV saline and one dose of zoledronate, with normalization of calcium and renal function by day 3. A CT scan of the body showed two osteolytic lesions of the left frontal and temporal skull bones, multiple hypodense micronodules in all hepatic segments, and multiple splenic nodules. Brain MRI demonstrated T2-hyperintense, T1-isointense, gadolinium-enhancing lesions in the same skull regions. A DEXA scan revealed osteopenia (lumbar spine T-score –2.4). Mammography, esophagogastroduodenoscopy, and colonoscopy were normal. Bone marrow biopsy and labial salivary gland histology were unremarkable. A percutaneous fine-needle aspiration of the liver showed noncaseating granulomatous hepatitis without malignancy. The intradermal tuberculin test was negative. During this period, hypercalcemia recurred, and two additional doses of zoledronate were administered 15 days apart despite initial correction.

vignette:
A 55-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and opioid use disorder presented with worsening abdominal distention and a 60-lb unintentional weight loss over 1 year, along with increasing difficulty with bowel movements. He denied melena, nausea, vomiting, fevers, flank pain, dysphagia, or odynophagia, and had no history of abdominal surgery.

Three weeks before admission, abdominal CT with contrast showed a small-bowel obstruction with a transition point in the right-mid abdomen and focal small-bowel wall thickening, plus mesenteric adenopathy. His symptoms improved without intervention, and he was discharged.

He returned 3 weeks later with diffuse abdominal pain. Repeat CT showed multiple dilated loops of small bowel with air-fluid levels. Colonoscopy revealed two polyps; cold-forceps biopsies showed non-specific chronic inflammation without features of inflammatory bowel disease. Video capsule endoscopy demonstrated erythematous gastritis, multiple small-bowel ulcers, and an atrophic duodenum. Two weeks later, double-balloon enteroscopy identified multiple jejunal strictures and areas suggestive of inflammatory bowel disease, and outpatient IBD management was planned.

Two months later, he presented with severe abdominal pain, new nausea, and vomiting. Abdominal radiographs suggested pneumoperitoneum. Exploratory laparotomy revealed a perforated ulcer in the terminal ileum, which was repaired, and a proximal Brooke ileostomy was created. Biopsies around the perforation showed ulcerated mucosa with non-specific chronic inflammation. He was discharged after a 21-day hospital stay.

One month later, he was re-hospitalized for non-specific abdominal symptoms and increased ostomy output. Ileoscopy showed scalloped mucosa with blunted villi throughout the ileum, and biopsies were taken. Histologic examination revealed extensive lymphocytic infiltrates with epitheliotropism but no definitive atypical morphological features, raising suspicion for a lymphoid neoplasm. A hematopathology consultation was obtained.

Biliary colic is pain from gallstone obstruction, which was explicitly ruled out by ultrasound showing no gallstones.
Myocardial infarction is ruled out by normal troponin and ECG findings not indicative of acute ischemia (sinus rhythm, LVH).

Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease (GERD) is a common cause of burning epigastric pain, but the severity of hypertension and the presence of pericardial effusion point away from GERD as the primary diagnosis in this acute presentation.

Pericarditis involves inflammation of the pericardium and can cause chest pain and pericardial effusion. While a pericardial effusion is noted, the severe hypertension and epigastric pain in the context of a potential vascular emergency make aortic dissection a more encompassing and critical diagnosis. Pericarditis is a possible complication or co-occurrence but not the primary diagnosis for the overall presentation.

A 33-year-old man with a history of massive small-bowel and ileocecal resection 12 years earlier (leaving 40 cm of small intestine) was maintained on a normal diet after bowel rehabilitation. One month before admission, he developed diarrhea and a 7-kg weight loss with progressive weakness, anorexia, dizziness, and cachexia. On admission his weight was 36 kg (BMI 12.2 kg/m^2), heart rate 80 bpm, blood pressure 70/50 mmHg, and respiratory rate 18 bpm. He was alert and oriented. Physical examination showed pitting edema of the lower extremities, thin skin, a scaphoid abdomen, and no ascites. Chest radiography revealed a dense nodule outside the right upper lung field (thought to be rib calcification). Lower-limb radiographs and renal ultrasonography were normal; gallbladder ultrasonography showed atrophy. ECG demonstrated normal sinus rhythm with T-wave flattening/inversion in leads II, III, aVF, and V4–V6, and an incomplete right bundle-branch block. Initial laboratory values included: phosphate 1.10 mmol/L, potassium 3.1 mmol/L, sodium 144 mmol/L, glucose 6.0 mmol/L, magnesium 0.60 mmol/L, calcium 1.7 mmol/L, albumin 27.7 g/L, prealbumin 100 mg/dL, hemoglobin 48 g/L, hematocrit 14.0%, BUN 5.0 mmol/L, and creatinine 86 mg/dL. Over 24 hours his strength and edema improved. Then he acutely developed profound fatigue and flaccid weakness of all four limbs. His heart rate was 98 bpm, respiratory rate was unchanged, and repeat labs showed a phosphate level of 0.05 mmol/L.

A 5-year-old boy with no prior medical history was noted by his parents to have a slowly developing limitation in right-eye movement over several weeks. There was no pain, inflammation, fever, trauma, or history of ocular infection, and his overall health was unchanged. On examination, abduction of the right eye was restricted. There were no signs of proptosis, strabismus, visual impairment, or inflammation in either eye; the remainder of the physical examination was normal. Noncontrast CT of the orbits showed a well-circumscribed extraconal mass at the right superolateral orbital wall, adjacent to the frontozygomatic suture, with smooth bone remodeling and fluid-attenuating content but no bone invasion. Subsequent MRI demonstrated a cystic mass in the right superior extraconal compartment that was hyperintense on T2-weighted images, hypointense on FLAIR imaging, and exhibited no diffusion restriction or internal enhancement after gadolinium administration. The lesion exerted mild compression on the external and superior rectus muscles, correlating with the abduction deficit, but did not involve the optic nerve, intraconal fat, or show intracranial extension.

raw.content:
A 44-year-old woman from Veracruz, Mexico, of low socioeconomic status, with systemic lupus erythematosus since 2003 (cutaneous, joint, and renal involvement), presented with a one-week history of progressive headache, phonophobia, high-grade fever, vomiting, and watery diarrhea. One month earlier, she had been treated for SLE-associated thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura with plasmapheresis, cyclophosphamide, and prednisone at 1 mg/kg per day.

On admission she had systemic inflammatory response syndrome and nuchal rigidity but no focal neurologic deficits or clinical signs of lupus activity. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 11.2 g/dL, MCV 103 fL, eosinophils 150 cells/mm3, creatinine 0.8 mg/dL, haptoglobin 77 mg/dL, ALT 59 IU/L, AST 78 IU/L, LDH 310 mg/dL, C3 96.5 mg/dL, lactate 0.9 mmol/L, and proteinuria 310 mg/day. Chest radiograph and head CT were unremarkable. Lumbar puncture revealed a pH of 7.35, glucose 45 mg/dL (serum glucose 130 mg/dL), protein 329 mg/dL, 42 white cells/mm3 (95% neutrophils), and 2 red cells/mm3. Cerebrospinal fluid culture grew Enterococcus gallinarum, and she was treated with intravenous ampicillin, with improvement in her neurologic symptoms.

On hospital day 3, she developed hemoptysis, bilateral patchy pulmonary infiltrates on chest radiograph, a drop in hemoglobin concentration, and acute respiratory failure requiring mechanical ventilation and ICU admission. Cultures were obtained, and she was started on methylprednisolone boluses and broad-spectrum antibiotics. The initial clinical diagnosis was diffuse alveolar hemorrhage caused by SLE activity without sufficient clinical criteria of nosocomial pneumonia.

On hospital day 4, she developed a purpuric skin rash, and a skin biopsy was performed.

A 38-year-old Indian man with a history of recurrent low-grade fevers and newly diagnosed diabetes mellitus treated with metformin presented with 10 days of right-sided chest and right upper abdominal pain and dyspnea. He described sharp, tearing, localized pain (7/10), worsened by movement and deep inspiration, without cough or hemoptysis. He denied gastrointestinal or urinary symptoms, sick contacts, recent travel, or asbestos exposure. He reported past extramarital sexual relationships. On admission: temperature 37.2°C; heart rate 110 bpm; blood pressure 130/80 mmHg; respiratory rate 40 breaths/min. Examination revealed a patchy, macular hyperpigmented rash on both shins and dorsum of the feet, and decreased breath sounds and vocal fremitus at the right lower chest. Laboratory studies showed white blood cell count 12.3 × 10^3/µL, hemoglobin 15 g/dL, platelets 219 × 10^3/µL; blood urea nitrogen 4.3 mmol/L; creatinine 69 µmol/L. Chest radiograph demonstrated patchy infiltrates in the right lower zone and obliteration of the right costophrenic angle. Thoracentesis yielded pale yellow fluid with 1260 WBCs/µL (87% neutrophils), 1590 RBCs/µL, pH 7.237; a rare giant cell was seen; cultures were negative. Pleural biopsy showed empyema without granulomas; Quantiferon and acid-fast bacilli studies were negative. CT chest revealed multiple encysted pleural effusions in the right lung. Transesophageal echocardiography showed no thrombi or intracardiac masses. A comprehensive respiratory viral and atypical pathogen panel was negative. The patient was treated sequentially with piperacillin/tazobactam and then meropenem, with gradual resolution of fever and clinical improvement; a chest tube and thoracotomy were performed to drain the effusion.

A 33-year-old woman presented with a 5-day history of gradually progressive swelling, pain, and stiffness in her left lower leg. She reported pain at rest and denied fever, chest pain, shortness of breath, hemoptysis, or syncope. Her medical history was notable for three prior abortions, recurrent microcytic anemia treated with iron supplementation, and two prior dilation and curettage procedures. She had no personal history of DVT and no family history of thromboembolic disease.

On examination, her temperature was afebrile, heart rate 85 bpm, blood pressure 125/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 100% on room air. Cardiopulmonary examination was unremarkable. The left lower leg was tender, swollen, warm, and erythematous. Bilateral dorsalis pedis pulses were palpable, and sensation was intact without ischemic changes.

Laboratory studies showed normal renal function, electrolytes, C3, C4, prothrombin time, and partial thromboplastin time; hemoglobin 9.5 g/dL with an MCV of 63 fL; C-reactive protein 4 mg/L (normal); and ESR 40 mm/hr (elevated). ECG and chest radiograph were normal. Doppler ultrasonography of the left lower extremity demonstrated extensive deep vein thrombosis. A porto-venous phase CT scan revealed compression of the left common iliac vein by the overlying right common iliac artery with a filling defect in the dilated, nonenhancing left common iliac vein. Given her obstetric history, tests for anti-beta-2-glycoprotein antibodies, lupus anticoagulant, and antiphospholipid antibodies were sent, all of which returned negative.

While it can present as multiple subcutaneous nodules, the cytological description (plump spindle cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, collagenous matrix, bipolar cytoplasmic extensions, inconspicuous nucleoli) is not typical for neurofibroma, which often shows wavy nuclei and a myxoid background.

While it shares some features with myofibromatosis (spindle cells, collagenous matrix), desmoid tumors are typically solitary, locally aggressive, and often involve deep soft tissues or abdominal wall, and are not typically multifocal subcutaneous lesions in a child as described. A 15-year-old girl presented with multiple swellings of five months’ duration. She noted progressive enlargement of bilateral neck masses and one each on her back and anterior abdominal wall, without pain. There was no significant past medical, personal, or family history. 

On examination, there were seven subcutaneous, nontender, mobile swellings measuring 1×1 to 3×3 cm in the cervical regions, right paraspinal area, and anterior abdominal wall. The lesions were firm to hard without changes in the overlying skin. 

Complete blood count, metabolic panel, and skeletal survey were all normal. With a clinical impression of lymphoreticular malignancy or metastatic disease, fine-needle aspiration cytology (FNAC) was performed on the most prominent swellings (two cervical, one paraspinal, one abdominal). 

Cytology smears from all sites showed moderate cellularity with similar features: predominantly plump spindle cells with abundant eosinophilic cytoplasm, fragments of collagenous matrix, and occasional small cells with scant cytoplasm. The spindle cells had bipolar cytoplasmic extensions and round-to-oval nuclei with fine granular chromatin; nucleoli were inconspicuous. Nuclear hyperchromasia, pleomorphism, or atypicality was not seen, and mitoses were sparse. There was no necrosis or inflammatory cells. 

Ultrasonography confirmed that all lesions were confined to the subcutaneous tissue, with no lymphadenopathy or deeper masses.

A 14-year-old Caucasian girl was transferred from a community emergency department after treatment for presumed anaphylaxis following ingestion of a hypoallergenic nutritional supplement. raw.content:
A 56-year-old African American woman with no significant past medical history presented with a six-day history of progressive swelling of the left labia, which ruptured and began draining serosanguinous fluid two days before admission. On arrival, her temperature was 36.8 °C, blood pressure 100/60 mmHg despite intravenous fluid resuscitation, pulse 96‒100 beats/min, respiratory rate 20 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Laboratory studies showed a white blood cell count of 17.4 × 10^9/L. Empiric intravenous vancomycin and piperacillin/tazobactam were initiated, and a surgical consultation was obtained. Pelvic CT imaging demonstrated an ulceration of the left labia with air in the subcutaneous fat of the left groin and lower abdominal wall, as well as inflammatory fat stranding along the left lateral abdominal wall. The Laboratory Risk Indicator for Necrotizing Fasciitis (LRINEC) score was calculated as 3, with the potential to rise to 7 pending C-reactive protein results. Despite non-definitive laboratory and imaging findings, concerns for sepsis, subcutaneous gas on CT, and the LRINEC score led to the decision to proceed with immediate exploratory surgery.

raw.content:
A 26-year-old woman presented with a 2-day history of burning on urination, urinary frequency, nocturia, and constant 5/10 suprapubic pain that did not radiate. She denied fever, nausea, vomiting, changes in bowel movements, weight change, palpitations, heat or cold intolerance, peripheral edema, and abnormal vaginal discharge. Her last menstrual period was one week earlier. Physical examination revealed lower abdominal tenderness, most pronounced in the para-umbilical area, without costovertebral angle tenderness.

Laboratory tests showed a negative serum β-hCG, normal CBC and BMP, and a urinalysis with 10–25 WBCs per high-power field, moderate bacteria, moderate mucus, moderate yeast, and positive nitrites; cervical NAAT was negative for Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis. A diagnosis of lower urinary tract infection was made, and she received a 10-day course of antibiotics as an outpatient.

Despite treatment, her dysuria, frequency, and burning worsened. She reported chronic constipation, with two hard, non-bloody stools per week managed intermittently with stool softeners. There was no history of abdominal trauma or family gastrointestinal disease. 

Because of persistent symptoms, a contrast-enhanced CT scan of the abdomen and pelvis was performed. It demonstrated a 4.0 × 3.3 × 6.8 cm multiloculated, enhancing hypodense and isodense mass extending superiorly from the dome of the bladder to the posterior surface of the umbilicus, with surrounding acute inflammatory stranding and minimal fluid. There was possible invasion into the bladder dome, secondary thickening of an adjacent distal small-bowel loop, and perivesical stranding around a thick-walled, collapsed bladder.

Given these findings, differential diagnoses included patent urachus, urachal sinus, urachal diverticulum, and malignant transformation of a urachal remnant, and diagnostic laparoscopy was planned.

A 36-year-old G5P2+2 woman with two prior cesarean deliveries and two first-trimester miscarriages was referred at 6 weeks of amenorrhea for evaluation of a pregnancy of unknown location. Her serum quantitative β-hCG was 16,124 mIU/mL. A transabdominal ultrasound at presentation did not locate an intrauterine or extrauterine pregnancy. A 32-year-old Caucasian woman presents with severe left knee pain and bilateral genu valgum deformity. She recalls being told she “may have had rickets” at age 9 but was lost to follow-up. • Total 25-hydroxyvitamin D and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D: elevated  
• Parathyroid hormone: low  
• FGF23: undetectable

A 49-year-old woman of African origin presented with a 10-year history of a right‐sided scalp mass that had been stable and nontender until it was excised at a peripheral clinic 5 months ago (no histopathology was done). Over the next 5 months, the lesion recurred, gradually enlarged, ulcerated, and bled easily. She denied headaches, convulsions, or neurologic deficits. On examination, she was afebrile and hemodynamically stable. There was no pallor, jaundice, or palpable peripheral lymphadenopathy. Local scalp examination revealed two lesions on the right side: a fungating, tender, 9 × 7 cm mass prone to bleeding and mild mobility, and a second non‐fungating, 3 × 3 cm lesion. Laboratory studies showed a normal complete blood count and basic metabolic panel. Chest radiography and abdominal/pelvic ultrasound were unremarkable. A head and neck CT scan demonstrated a multilobulated, hyperdense, ulcerative right frontal scalp lesion measuring 9 × 7.8 × 6 cm without skull bone erosion or intracranial extension, along with enlarged cervical lymph nodes at levels I and II. MRI of the spine revealed a pathological compression fracture of T10 and a hyperintense lesion in T8, raising suspicion for vertebral metastases. Clinical staging was considered stage IVc.

raw.content:
A 56-year-old woman with no significant medical history presented with a 4-week history of dry cough and mild weight loss. She denied fever, haemoptysis, night sweats, and had no known contacts with tuberculosis. Two courses of antibiotics produced no improvement. On examination, coarse crepitations were heard over the right upper and lower lung zones. A chest radiograph showed an air-space opacity in the right upper lobe. CT of the thorax demonstrated multifocal consolidations in the right upper lobe extending to the right lower lobe. Given the clinical and radiographic suspicion for pulmonary tuberculosis, she was started empirically on anti-tuberculosis therapy. After 2 weeks, her symptoms persisted. A Mantoux tuberculin skin test showed 10 mm of induration. Sputum induction for acid-fast bacilli was negative, and bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for Xpert® Mycobacterium tuberculosis/rifampicin assay as well as bacterial and fungal cultures. Hence, a CT-guided lung biopsy was planned.

raw.content:
A 9-year-old boy was referred with left cheek swelling and hyperglobus of the left eye. Hyperglobus was first noted about 1 year earlier under ophthalmologic observation. Six months later, swelling of the left cheek developed, with marked progression over the preceding 3 months. 

On extraoral examination, there was a painless, bony-hard swelling of the left cheek. The overlying skin was normal, but the patient reported numbness of the left cheek and weakness in movement of the left upper lip. There were no other neurologic deficits, no visual disturbances, and ocular motility was intact. Intraoral examination revealed expansion of the left maxillary ridge with mobility of primary teeth c, d, and e.

A panoramic radiograph and cone-beam computed tomography demonstrated a large, well-circumscribed, expansile, heterogeneous (mixed-density) mass occupying the entire left maxillary sinus. The lesion caused deviation and destruction of the nasal septum, invaded the ethmoid sinus, thinned, displaced, and perforated the anterior wall of the sphenoid sinus, extended into the pterygopalatine fossa with destruction of the pterygoid plates, and elevated and perforated the left infraorbital rim. There was extreme postero-superior displacement of the second molar toward the inferior orbital fissure, resulting in blockage of the fissure, and compromise of the nasopharyngeal space.

Medical history was notable for seasonal allergic reactions and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency; blood pressure was documented as 10/5 mmHg. Coagulation studies were within normal limits. Laboratory evaluation showed WBC 19 × 10³/μl, RBC 3.66 × 10⁶/μl, hemoglobin 10.6 g/dl, hematocrit 33.2%, and MCHC 31.9 g/dl; other serum chemistries were normal.

An intraoral incisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia with mepivacaine to minimize the risk of methemoglobinemia.

strict_audit_context.vignette:
A 9-year-old boy was referred with left cheek swelling and hyperglobus of the left eye. Hyperglobus was first noted about 1 year earlier under ophthalmologic observation. Six months later, swelling of the left cheek developed, with marked progression over the preceding 3 months. 

On extraoral examination, there was a painless, bony-hard swelling of the left cheek. The overlying skin was normal, but the patient reported numbness of the left cheek and weakness in movement of the left upper lip. There were no other neurologic deficits, no visual disturbances, and ocular motility was intact. Intraoral examination revealed expansion of the left maxillary ridge with mobility of primary teeth c, d, and e.

A panoramic radiograph and cone-beam computed tomography demonstrated a large, well-circumscribed, expansile, heterogeneous (mixed-density) mass occupying the entire left maxillary sinus. The lesion caused deviation and destruction of the nasal septum, invaded the ethmoid sinus, thinned, displaced, and perforated the anterior wall of the sphenoid sinus, extended into the pterygopalatine fossa with destruction of the pterygoid plates, and elevated and perforated the left infraorbital rim. There was extreme postero-superior displacement of the second molar toward the inferior orbital fissure, resulting in blockage of the fissure, and compromise of the nasopharyngeal space.

Medical history was notable for seasonal allergic reactions and glucose-6-phosphate dehydrogenase deficiency; blood pressure was documented as 10/5 mmHg. Coagulation studies were within normal limits. Laboratory evaluation showed WBC 19 × 10³/μl, RBC 3.66 × 10⁶/μl, hemoglobin 10.6 g/dl, hematocrit 33.2%, and MCHC 31.9 g/dl; other serum chemistries were normal.

An intraoral incisional biopsy was performed under local anesthesia with mepivacaine to minimize the risk of methemoglobinemia.

raw.content:
A 59‐year‐old Japanese woman was referred for 6 weeks of bilateral posterior ankle pain and anterior knee pain, and 4 weeks of pain in the metacarpophalangeal joint of the left third finger. She had been diagnosed with hypertension and heterozygous familial hypercholesterolemia (HeFH) at age 57, with an initial LDL‐C of 359 mg/dL, reduced to ~170 mg/dL on pitavastatin and ezetimibe for the past 6 months. She had no personal or family history of rheumatoid arthritis. On examination, she had bilateral arcus corneae; swelling and thickening of the midportion of both Achilles tendons with tenderness to palpation extending to the calcaneal insertion; tenderness over both tibial tuberosities and the right medial humeral epicondyle; and tenderness of the first and fifth right MTP joints and the second left MTP joint. The right third and right second MCP joints were swollen dorsally, and a nodule was noted on the extensor tendon of the right third digit. Laboratory studies showed an ESR of 118 mm/h, CRP 2.06 mg/dL, rheumatoid factor 49.3 U/mL (normal <15), anti‐CCP2 >300 U/mL (normal <4.5), and MMP‐3 62.3 ng/mL (normal <59.7). Radiographs of the hands, feet, ankles, and knees showed no erosions or enthesophytes, although the ankle films demonstrated soft‐tissue widening suggestive of Achilles tendon thickening. Musculoskeletal ultrasound revealed the following:
- Achilles tendons: markedly swollen, rounded cross‐section; inhomogeneous, hypoechoic with loss of fibrillar pattern; power Doppler showed markedly increased vascularity inside and around the tendon, with vessels entering from the ventral aspect via Kager’s fat; no paratenon thickening, bursitis, or bony irregularity.  
- Patellar tendons: focal thickening of the distal tendon, inhomogeneous hypoechoic with loss of fibrillar pattern; power Doppler showed increased flow in hypoechoic areas; no bursitis or bony changes; mild suprapatellar synovitis.  
- Finger extensor tendons at the right third and left second and fourth MCP joints: focal thickening, hypoechoic with loss of fibrillar pattern; power Doppler showed increased flow; mild synovitis in the right second MCP joint.  
- Feet: synovial thickening with hyperemia in the first, second, third, and fifth MTP joints of the right foot and the first and second MTP joints of the left foot.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

An 89-year-old woman with persistent atrial fibrillation (not anticoagulated) and hypertension presented with acute speech disturbance and right-sided weakness. On examination she was alert, had global aphasia, right facial asymmetry, right upper- and lower-limb paresis with decreased tone, and a right Babinski sign; NIH Stroke Scale score was 19. She had no history of COVID-19, and two mRNA vaccine doses; RT-PCR testing for SARS-CoV-2 on admission and hospital day 3 was negative. 

Noncontrast head CT showed early ischemic changes in the left insula and frontal lobe. CT angiography revealed acute occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery at M1/M2 and chronic occlusion of the left internal carotid artery; an incidental mass in the left orbit was also noted. She received intravenous thrombolysis with reperfusion of the left ICA. Conventional angiography confirmed left MCA occlusion and restored flow in the ICA and ACA. Mechanical thrombectomy achieved angiographic reperfusion of the MCA but no clinical improvement; follow-up CT confirmed an infarct in the left MCA territory. 

Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral oval lesions in the medial orbits, which were initially interpreted as orbital tumors. CT angiography of the chest showed pulmonary emboli in segmental arteries of the right lower lobe. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, degenerative mitral and aortic valves, and severe low-gradient aortic stenosis with preserved ejection fraction. Twenty-four-hour Holter monitoring confirmed atrial fibrillation; ambulatory blood pressure monitoring was normal. 

Laboratory studies showed elevated C-reactive protein (10.74 mg/dL) and procalcitonin (0.11 ng/mL) with normal renal, liver function, and electrolytes. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed mild pleocytosis (10 cells/µL) and elevated protein (55 mg/dL) with normal glucose. Multiple blood and urine cultures were negative, and repeat SARS-CoV-2 testing was negative. Vasculitic, autoimmune, viral infection, and malignancy screens were unremarkable, and rheumatology and angiology consultations excluded systemic vasculitis, neoplasm, and histiocytosis.

On examination she was alert, had global aphasia, right facial asymmetry, right upper- and lower-limb paresis with decreased tone, and a right Babinski sign; NIH Stroke Scale score was 19. She had no history of COVID-19, and two mRNA vaccine doses; RT-PCR testing for SARS-CoV-2 on admission and hospital day 3 was negative. 

Noncontrast head CT showed early ischemic changes in the left insula and frontal lobe. CT angiography revealed acute occlusion of the left middle cerebral artery at M1/M2 and chronic occlusion of the left internal carotid artery; an incidental mass in the left orbit was also noted. She received intravenous thrombolysis with reperfusion of the left ICA. Conventional angiography confirmed left MCA occlusion and restored flow in the ICA and ACA. Mechanical thrombectomy achieved angiographic reperfusion of the MCA but no clinical improvement; follow-up CT confirmed an infarct in the left MCA territory. 

Brain MRI demonstrated bilateral oval lesions in the medial orbits, which were initially interpreted as orbital tumors. CT angiography of the chest showed pulmonary emboli in segmental arteries of the right lower lobe. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, degenerative mitral and aortic valves, and severe low-gradient aortic stenosis with preserved ejection fraction. Twenty-four-hour Holter monitoring confirmed atrial fibrillation; ambulatory blood pressure monitoring was normal. 

Laboratory studies showed elevated C-reactive protein (10.74 mg/dL) and procalcitonin (0.11 ng/mL) with normal renal, liver function, and electrolytes. Cerebrospinal fluid analysis revealed mild pleocytosis (10 cells/µL) and elevated protein (55 mg/dL) with normal glucose. Multiple blood and urine cultures were negative, and repeat SARS-CoV-2 testing was negative. Vasculitic, autoimmune, viral infection, and malignancy screens were unremarkable, and rheumatology and angiology consultations excluded systemic vasculitis, neoplasm, and histiocytosis.
