raw.content:
A 40-year-old man presented with 5 days of progressive dyspnea. On day 1 he was short of breath only with uphill walking (MMRC grade 1), by day 2 he was breathless on level ground (grade 2), and by day 4 he was dyspneic at rest (grade 4). He also noted central, nonradiating chest pain with coughing, without positional change. He denied fever, night sweats, cyanosis, grunting, palpitations, or hemoptysis. He had three previous hospital admissions, most recently 4 months earlier for acute severe pancreatitis. He had a 5-year history of local alcohol consumption but had abstained for 6 months. 

On examination, pulse was 116/min, respiratory rate 30/min, blood pressure 110/70 mmHg, temperature 98 °F, and SpO2 95% on 4 L O2 by nasal prong. He had bilateral pitting edema to the knees. Chest inspection showed decreased movement on the left; trachea deviated rightward; decreased fremitus and stony dullness over the entire left hemithorax; and absent breath sounds on the left. Cardiovascular and abdominal examinations were unremarkable; there were no stigmata of chronic liver disease.

Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 9.7 g/dL, WBC 5530/mm3, CRP 73.9 mg/L, alkaline phosphatase 145 U/L, serum albumin 3.1 g/dL, serum amylase 486 U/L, and lipase 416 U/L. 

Chest radiograph revealed complete opacification of the left hemithorax with tracheal shift to the right, consistent with massive left pleural effusion. 

Ultrasonography of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis confirmed a large left pleural effusion with passive basal lung collapse, and showed a normal-sized pancreas with heterogeneous echotexture and a small intrapancreatic collection at the tail. 

Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated multiple non-enhancing cystic areas in the pancreas (largest 23×16 mm in the tail), minimal peripancreatic fat stranding, and no main pancreatic duct dilation or parenchymal calcifications. 

Diagnostic thoracentesis yielded 900 mL of dark brown, turbid fluid. Pleural fluid analysis: protein 3.5 g/dL; LDH 1413 U/L; glucose 98 mg/dL; ADA 31.4 U/L; total cell count 100/mm3 (10% neutrophils, 90% lymphocytes); amylase 11,871 U/L; PCV 0.8%; no malignant cells; culture negative; MTB/RIF PCR negative.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 19-year-old woman presented with an 18-month history of pain in the plantar aspect of her left foot.  The pain was moderate initially, often worse at night, and markedly exacerbated by compression and exposure to cold.  Over the past four months, the patient noted aggravation of the local pain and was referred for imaging.  She denied any trauma and had no family history of neurofibromatosis.  

On examination, three prominent, soft-tissue nodules with swelling and tenderness were palpated in the plantar aspect of the left foot; they were mobile and not adherent to surrounding tissue.  Sensation testing revealed numbness in the medial distal plantar foot; toe and foot motor strength were normal.  

Magnetic resonance imaging of the left foot demonstrated three nodules arranged in a linear distribution in the mid-plantar region.  On T1-weighted images, the lesions were homogeneously isointense to skeletal muscle.  On T2-weighted fat-suppressed images, they were homogeneously hyperintense without cystic degeneration; each was surrounded by a hyperintense rim.  A small extension of high signal from the lateral aspect of one lesion resembled a “mouse-tail.”  Two nodules were located within the flexor digitorum brevis muscle beneath the plantar aponeurosis, and one was in the superficial fascia at the third metatarsophalangeal joint.  The lesions followed the course of branches of the common plantar digital nerves without evidence of invasion.  

Based on the clinical presentation and imaging findings, the differential diagnosis included glomus tumor, neurofibroma, and schwannoma.  Multiple plexiform schwannoma was suspected, and surgical excision was recommended.

vignette:
A 50-year-old man with a remote history of treated Lyme disease, and no hypertension, hyperlipidemia, or diabetes, presented after four episodes of syncope over 24 hours. Six weeks earlier, he had a syncope while exercising; initial workup was unrevealing. Outpatient ECG then showed a new left bundle branch block. Exercise stress testing provoked presyncope with a brief burst of atrial tachycardia. A pharmacological nuclear stress test demonstrated an LVEF of 42% with a moderate-size area of inferior wall ischaemia and scar, but he had no chest pain or heart failure symptoms.

On current presentation, vital signs were blood pressure 140/66 mmHg, heart rate 54 bpm, respiratory rate 18 breaths/min, temperature 36.2°C, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. Physical examination was unremarkable. A 12-lead ECG showed sinus rhythm at 57 bpm, first-degree AV block, and a prolonged QTc. He had a brief burst of atrial tachycardia that resolved with IV metoprolol. Cardiac enzymes, thyroid function tests, serum calcium, and ACE levels were normal. Lyme antibody testing was negative. Chest radiograph was normal. Transthoracic echocardiography showed an LVEF of 45–50% with no regional wall motion abnormalities. Telemetry captured intermittent high-grade AV block with ventricular escape beats, prompting placement of a temporary transvenous pacemaker.

Coronary angiography revealed normal coronary arteries, and left ventriculography showed an LVEF of 35–40%. A permanent dual-chamber pacemaker was implanted, and he was discharged on guideline-directed medical therapy for heart failure.

Outpatient cardiac magnetic resonance imaging demonstrated an LVEF of 31%, RV ejection fraction of 23%, and mid-myocardial late gadolinium enhancement in the basal anteroseptal wall. A contrast-enhanced CT scan of the chest showed mediastinal and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy.

candidate_relations.reason: Evans Syndrome is autoimmune hemolytic anemia and immune thrombocytopenia. The patient has pancytopenia, not just hemolytic anemia and thrombocytopenia. The reference diagnosis is Hairy Cell Leukemia.

Sweet's Syndrome is a skin condition characterized by fever, neutrophilia, and tender red plaques. The patient developed Sweet's syndrome postpartum, but the reference diagnosis is Hairy Cell Leukemia, which is a hematologic malignancy that can be associated with Sweet's syndrome, but Sweet's syndrome itself is not the most likely diagnosis for the overall clinical picture including pancytopenia. The question asks for the most likely diagnosis, not a co-occurring condition.

Systemic Lupus Erythematosus is a chronic autoimmune disease. While the patient has a family history of SLE and some features like pancytopenia could be seen, the overall picture and the reference diagnosis of Hairy Cell Leukemia make SLE unrelated as the most likely diagnosis.

Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura (TTP) is a rare blood disorder characterized by blood clots in small blood vessels. The patient does not present with the classic pentad of TTP (fever, neurologic symptoms, renal dysfunction, microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia). The reference diagnosis is Hairy Cell Leukemia.

Immune Thrombocytopenic Purpura (ITP) is a disorder that can lead to easy bruising and bleeding due to low platelet counts. While the patient was initially given a presumptive diagnosis of ITP in pregnancy, her persistent pancytopenia and the development of Sweet's syndrome point to a more systemic underlying condition, which is Hairy Cell Leukemia as per the reference diagnosis.

Antiphospholipid Syndrome is an autoimmune disorder characterized by blood clots and pregnancy complications. The patient does not have a history of recurrent thrombosis or specific pregnancy complications associated with APS. The reference diagnosis is Hairy Cell Leukemia.

Hemolytic Uremic Syndrome (HUS) is a condition characterized by hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury. The patient does not have significant renal involvement or clear evidence of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. The reference diagnosis is Hairy Cell Leukemia.
Neonatal Alloimmune Thrombocytopenia (NAIT) affects the neonate, not the mother. The neonate's platelet count was normal. The reference diagnosis is Hairy Cell Leukemia.

Pregnancy-Associated Thrombocytopenia is a common and usually mild condition. The patient's pancytopenia and the development of Sweet's syndrome suggest a more serious underlying condition than simple pregnancy-associated thrombocytopenia. The reference diagnosis is Hairy Cell Leukemia.

HELLP Syndrome (Hemolysis, Elevated Liver enzymes, Low Platelet count) is a severe complication of pregnancy. While the patient had low platelets, she did not have elevated liver enzymes or clear evidence of hemolysis. The reference diagnosis is Hairy Cell Leukemia.

A 37-year-old woman, gravida 2 para 1, was found on routine blood screening at 10 weeks’ gestation to have pancytopenia: platelet count 85×10^9/L, white-cell count 2.3×10^9/L (neutrophils 1.3×10^9/L, monocytes 0.2×10^9/L), and hemoglobin 10.6 g/dL. She reported occasional easy bruising over the prior two months but no bleeding, lymphadenopathy, or splenomegaly. Her only prior pregnancy, 13 months earlier, was uncomplicated with normal platelet counts. She had equivocal hypothyroidism, a family history of thyroid disease and systemic lupus erythematosus, and no new medications. Thyroid function, immunoglobulins, folate, and vitamin B12 were normal; antinuclear antibody was negative. Ferritin was low, and iron supplements were started.

She was given a presumptive diagnosis of immune thrombocytopenia in pregnancy. Her fatigue persisted but she had no bleeding complications. At 38 weeks’ gestation, with a platelet count of 61×10^9/L, prednisolone 20 mg daily was initiated without response (platelets 65×10^9/L), followed by intravenous immunoglobulin at 1 g/kg (platelets 52×10^9/L). She underwent spontaneous vaginal delivery at 38 weeks with minor bleeding; her platelet count was 52×10^9/L, and the neonate’s platelet count was normal.

Five weeks postpartum, she developed a pustular rash on the left upper arm, abdomen, and back. Skin biopsy showed dermal neutrophils with upper dermal edema and a subepidermal blister, consistent with bullous Sweet’s syndrome. Her blood counts remained low: hemoglobin 13.0 g/dL, white-cell count 1.7×10^9/L (neutrophils 0.5×10^9/L, monocytes 0.1×10^9/L), and platelets 49×10^9/L.

MR is a male neonate born at 38 weeks’ gestation by elective cesarean delivery. Birth weight was 2350 g (5th–10th percentile), length 45 cm (5th percentile), head circumference 31 cm (<5th percentile). Apgar scores were 8 and 9 at 1 and 5 minutes.

Fetal ultrasound at 20 weeks suggested intracranial hemorrhage, confirmed by fetal MRI at 25 weeks, which showed a 2.3 cm porencephalic cyst in the right frontotemporal–insular region with ex vacuo enlargement of the right lateral ventricle, reduced right cerebral hemisphere volume, and abnormal micropolygyria of the right frontal cortex.

Gene sequencing for MTHFR and factor V Leiden was wild type. Newborn metabolic screening was negative.

A 53-year-old man was admitted for progressive dyspnea (NYHA class III). His history included a congenital ventricular septal defect repaired in childhood, subsequent aortic valve and septal patch replacements, permanent atrial fibrillation on anticoagulation, chronic hepatitis C–related liver disease, and prior admission for heart failure with preserved ejection fraction. On examination, he had jugular venous distension, irregular rhythm, a 2/6 systolic murmur at the aortic and mitral areas, decreased breath sounds at the right lung base, and peripheral edema.  
ECG showed atrial fibrillation with left bundle branch block. Chest radiography demonstrated pulmonary congestion and a right basal pleural effusion. Transthoracic echocardiography revealed: a dilated left ventricle with preserved ejection fraction (60%), a dilated right ventricle with normal systolic function, no residual septal shunt, a normally functioning mechanical aortic prosthesis but elevated transprosthetic gradients (mean 33 mmHg) with an effective orifice area index of 0.4 cm2/m2 (suggesting severe prosthesis–patient mismatch), moderate mitral regurgitation, severe tricuspid regurgitation, and estimated systolic pulmonary artery pressure of 50 mmHg. The inferior vena cava was dilated with poor inspiratory collapse.  
An initial diagnosis of heart failure with preserved ejection fraction was made, and intravenous diuretics led to reduction of edema and resolution of radiographic congestion, but the patient remained dyspneic with low exercise tolerance and still required supplemental oxygen.  
A contrast CT scan of the chest and abdomen showed a small right pleural effusion, no lung parenchymal disease or pulmonary embolism, cirrhotic liver with a focal lesion suspicious for hepatocellular carcinoma, splenomegaly, and signs of portal hypertension.  
Right heart catheterization revealed a high cardiac output state, normal pulmonary vascular resistance, and only a slight elevation of mean pulmonary and wedge pressures.

vignette:
A 14-year-old girl presented to the emergency department with a worsening facial rash that began 6 days earlier. It initially appeared as red papules over the left cheek; her pediatrician prescribed acyclovir for presumed eczema herpeticum and instructed her to discontinue all topical products. Over the next 3 days, the rash progressed markedly, and she was brought to the hospital. 

Her medical history was notable only for a nonspecific facial rash of 2 years’ duration on both cheeks, diagnosed as atopic dermatitis and treated with triamcinolone 0.1% ointment twice daily. She had been applying this ointment to her face at least daily for 2 years, pausing for no more than 1–2 days at a time because the rash promptly returned. She stopped the ointment completely 3 days before presentation. She denied fever, systemic symptoms, or personal or family history of atopy.

On examination, she was afebrile and appeared well. There were confluent erythematous, edematous plaques in the bilateral periorbital areas (left more than right), studded with numerous 2– to 3-mm pustules, some coalescing into “lakes of pus.” A few pustules were also noted in the perioral area. A 59-year-old man with a history of diabetes mellitus presented with one day of left-sided weakness, left facial paresis, difficulty speaking, and drowsiness. His NIH Stroke Scale score on admission was 10. He denied recent head trauma or family history of stroke or thrombosis. He was a non-smoker but used opiates.  

On examination, he was confused and could not follow commands. Temperature was 37.4 °C, blood pressure 150/90 mm Hg, heart rate 73 bpm, respiratory rate 16/min, and oxygen saturation 97% on room air. There was no pallor, jaundice, petechiae, or organomegaly. Cranial-nerve exam was normal except for left facial paresis. Motor testing showed left hemiparesis (3/5 in the arm, 4/5 in the leg) with decreased pain response on the left and an upgoing plantar response on that side.  

An ECG showed normal sinus rhythm. A noncontrast head CT performed >24 h after symptom onset revealed an acute right MCA territory infarct in the right parietotemporal lobe. Twenty-four hours later, because of worsening consciousness, a repeat CT showed a new infarct in the left frontal lobe (left MCA territory).  

Initial laboratory results included a platelet count of 77 × 10^3/μL and hemoglobin 15 g/dL. Over the next several days, the platelet count declined to 21 × 10^3/μL, and hemoglobin fell to 11.8 g/dL. Reticulocytes were 2.6%, LDH was 1148 U/L, total bilirubin rose from 1.9 mg/dL to 4.4 mg/dL (indirect bilirubin 3.1 mg/dL), and acute-phase reactants (ESR, CRP, ferritin, fibrinogen, D-dimer) were elevated. Coagulation studies, troponin, liver function tests, lipid profile, and electrolytes were within normal limits. Peripheral blood smear showed occasional schistocytes. Direct and indirect Coombs tests were negative.

raw.content:
An 80-year-old woman with a history of rectal cancer treated in 2008 by liver metastasectomy followed by Hartmann’s procedure with intraoperative radiotherapy (5×5 Gy) and adjuvant capecitabine, oxaliplatin, and bevacizumab presented in January 2011 with intermittent gross hematuria. Since December 2009 she had bilateral JJ stents for ureteral strictures, replaced regularly. In November 2010 she required drainage of a pelvic abscess after stent occlusion complicated by Candida glabrata infection. Her medical history also included type 2 diabetes mellitus and angina pectoris.

On presentation, her hemoglobin was 7.2 mmol/L and creatinine was 370 μmol/L. Renal ultrasound showed bilateral hydronephrosis. Because of persistent hematuria and suspected stent occlusion, cystoscopy and ureteral stent exchange were performed: removal of the right double-J catheter revealed pulsatile arterial bleeding from the right ureteral orifice. The stent was changed, bleeding subsided, and she received four units of packed red cells intraoperatively. Open surgery was considered too high risk.

A CT angiogram demonstrated active hemorrhage at the right renal pelvis with clots in the collecting system. The patient was hemodynamically stable and managed expectantly, but that night she had recurrent gross hematuria. Embolisation of the right renal artery with coils was performed. During subsequent left stent repositioning, retrograde ureterography revealed a ureteroileal fistula, and a new ureteral catheter was placed; conservative management was advised. Within 24 hours, massive hematuria recurred and her hemoglobin continued to fall despite further transfusion.

A 36-year-old woman presented with a 7-day history of right-sided chest pain and dyspnea without fever or cough. She reported two prior spontaneous pneumothoraces: one right-sided in 2018 managed medically, and one left-sided in 2019 treated surgically. She also noted occasional small-volume hemoptysis. 

On admission, she was alert, with SpO2 97% on room air. Right chest auscultation revealed hypoventilation; no crackles were appreciated. The remainder of the examination, including endocrine and genitourinary systems, was unremarkable. 

Laboratory studies (CBC, chemistry, urinalysis) were within normal limits; microbiological tests for tuberculosis and other bacteria were negative. 

Chest radiography showed lung hyperinflation without focal parenchymal abnormalities. HRCT of the chest revealed a small right pneumothorax and numerous round, thin-walled air cysts (2–5 mm) scattered in both lungs; no irregular cyst shapes were noted. 

Pulmonary function testing demonstrated a 6-minute walk distance of 67% predicted, normal DLCO, and a negative bronchodilator response. 

Thirteen days later, she developed left-sided chest pain and dyspnea. Chest X-ray confirmed a new left pneumothorax; CT again showed a large left pneumothorax with passive atelectasis and persistent small air cysts bilaterally. Thoracoscopic surgery with pleural drainage was performed, and lung biopsies were obtained. 

Three months later, she had bilateral pneumothoraces requiring a third thoracoscopic intervention. One month after discharge, repeat CT showed resolution of pneumothorax, persistent small air cysts, and faint nodular infiltrates in both lower lobes.

An 80-year-old woman was referred for management of a chronic superficial sacral wound present for approximately 2 years. She reported progressively worsening sacral pain and local skin irritation but denied purulent discharge, altered bowel habits, rectal bleeding, or rectal discharge. On examination, she was afebrile and systemically well. The coccygectomy scar was slightly indurated and surrounded by a broad area of excoriated skin with plaques and focal ulceration in the upper natal cleft. A small superior sinus tract without obvious pits and mild serous discharge were noted. The lesion was located more than 5 cm from the anal verge. There was no exophytic mass, no underlying abscess cavity, and no palpable inguinal lymphadenopathy.

Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis with contrast demonstrated a 6 × 13 × 28 mm area of nonspecific, irregular superficial enhancement in the natal cleft without invasion of underlying structures, no visible sinus tract, and no regional nodal or bony metastases. A staging CT scan of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis showed no metastatic disease.

A 1-year-old girl was brought with sudden onset of hematemesis; the vomitus resembled coffee grounds. She was born full-term, had no significant medical or family history, no allergies, and no medication use, including NSAIDs. On arrival she was lethargic; temperature 36.8 °C, heart rate 160 bpm, respiratory rate 24 bpm, blood pressure 83/35 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 100% on 2 L nasal oxygen. Physical examination showed pallor but was otherwise unremarkable. A nasogastric tube aspirated a small amount of blood. Laboratory tests revealed WBC 9,500/μL; hemoglobin 7.2 g/dL; platelets 220×10^3/μL; CRP 0.55 mg/dL; normal liver function tests; prothrombin time 13.2 s (INR 1.01); aPTT 31.7 s; normal factor XIII and plasma gastrin levels; ESR 2 mm/h. Serologies for cytomegalovirus-IgM, EBV-VCA-IgM, and H. pylori-IgG were negative, and stool antigen testing excluded H. pylori. Blood cultures and stool parasite testing were negative. Abdominal radiography and ultrasonography were normal, and contrast-enhanced CT showed no active bleeding. She received two units of packed red blood cells and famotidine, yet her hemoglobin remained low. Thus, on hospital day 2, early upper endoscopy was planned to identify the bleeding source.

A 62-year-old man was admitted on June 25, 2021, with a 20-day history of episodic slurred speech that had worsened over the previous 9 days. Initially, episodes lasted about 10 minutes without loss of consciousness, headache, dizziness, diplopia, dysphagia, or limb weakness; by presentation, they occurred 2–3 times daily lasting about 30 minutes. His medical history included hypertension (>20 years), diabetes mellitus (8 years), and coronary heart disease (8 years); he was blind bilaterally after retinal detachment in adolescence. He denied smoking and alcohol use. On examination, temperature was 36.5°C, heart rate 70/min, respiratory rate 17/min, and blood pressure 144/86 mmHg. Cranial nerve exam showed dysarthria and midline tongue extension; limb strength was 5/5 with normal tone; Babinski and other reflexes were normal; he had no light perception with irregular pupils and absent light reflexes. Routine blood tests, coagulation studies, rheumatologic panels, thyroid function, tumor markers, liver and kidney function, and electrolytes were all normal. Brain MRI and susceptibility-weighted imaging were unremarkable; MRA showed mild cerebral arteriosclerosis; carotid MRA showed carotid arteriosclerosis with limited stenosis of the intracranial left vertebral artery; transcranial Doppler was normal. The initial diagnosis was transient ischemic attack of the vertebrobasilar system. On review, symptoms did not improve with rest; a fatigue test and a neostigmine test were both negative.

raw.content:
A 4-year-old girl of Turkish ancestry was brought to the emergency department for progressive unsteadiness and recurrent falls over the preceding 5 days. Five days earlier she had first noted staggering and grabbing for support to avoid falls; during her initial fall she sustained a nasal bridge laceration that required suturing. There was no prior medical history. On examination she was alert (GCS 15), afebrile, and appeared well; the nasal bridge wound was clean. Both external ear canals were obstructed by effusion and cerumen; the remainder of the neurologic and physical examination, including cranial-nerve testing, was age-appropriate. Routine blood tests were unremarkable.  
 Three-month history of “ear problems” was elicited: initial diagnosis of otitis media with effusion and tympanic perforation treated with antibiotics led to partial resolution. On current otoscopic examination, the left tympanic membrane was intact without effusion; the right external canal was occluded by polypoid tissue and purulent secretion. A Frenzel’s examination showed no nystagmus.  
 Contrast-enhanced CT of the head and temporal bones revealed bilateral osteolysis of the mastoids, superior and lateral semicircular canals, and the right external auditory canal, plus a separate osteolytic lesion in the dorsal left parietal bone. There was also adenoid hypertrophy and mild sinus mucosal thickening.  
 Brainstem evoked response audiometry demonstrated a threshold of 40 dB with normal wave latencies on the left and an 80 dB threshold with prolonged wave I latency on the right, indicating profound right-sided hearing loss.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

An 86-year-old woman with a history of dementia, living in a non–air-conditioned room during a heat wave, was found unconscious and brought to the emergency department. On arrival, her Glasgow Coma Scale score was 6 (E1V1M4), body temperature 42.4 °C, blood pressure 88/40 mm Hg, and pulse rate 120 beats/min. Laboratory studies revealed hepatic dysfunction, renal dysfunction, and disseminated intravascular coagulation. Head MRI and MRA showed no abnormality. She was diagnosed with severe heat stroke (APACHE II score 42, SOFA score 15), intubated, and treated with extracorporeal cooling, fluid resuscitation, and DIC therapy; fursultiamine and levothyroxine were also given. Despite treatment, she remained unconscious. On day 6, brain MRI showed bilateral cerebellar hemisphere high-signal intensity on diffusion-weighted and FLAIR images with corresponding low ADC signals. On day 9, SPECT with 123I-IMP demonstrated decreased perfusion in the right cerebellar hemisphere. By day 13, MRI abnormalities had begun to improve, and her level of consciousness improved to E4VTM6.

raw.content:
An 18-year-old African male with no prior medical history presented first with a 2-day history of tonsillitis and a new macular rash on his chest that extended to his arms. Three days later he developed abdominal cramping and multiple episodes of non-bloody, watery diarrhea without nausea or vomiting, along with fevers and joint pains in his wrists, elbows, and knees. Initial outpatient care included oral chlorhexidine, lozenges, and symptomatic treatment.

He was then seen at a local health facility with high fever, tachycardia, and within 24 hours became confused with rising serum creatinine (from 200 to 400 μmol/L). He received ceftriaxone, paracetamol, loperamide, and one dose of IV methylprednisolone, but continued to deteriorate and was transferred to our hospital.

On arrival he was febrile (40°C), hypotensive (70/40 mmHg), tachycardic (130 bpm), tachypneic (50 breaths/min), and hypoxemic (SaO2 86% on room air). GCS was 14/15. Lung exam revealed bilaterally coarse crepitations; cardiovascular exam an audible S3 gallop; abdomen distended and tense with hypoactive bowel sounds; musculoskeletal exam was normal. He received fluid resuscitation, central line placement, and norepinephrine at 0.4 μg/kg/min.

Laboratory data showed: WBC 27.1×10^9/L; Hb 10.9 g/dL; platelets 281×10^9/L; procalcitonin 71.6 ng/mL; CRP 287 mg/L; creatinine 494 μmol/L; urea 26.7 mmol/L; Na 128 mmol/L; K 4.87 mmol/L; HCO3– 15.5 mmol/L; blood gas pH 7.33, PCO2 23 mmHg, PO2 122 mmHg, HCO3– 19.8 mmol/L. Liver tests showed AST 1461 U/L and ALT 812 U/L; hepatitis A, B, C, and HIV screens were negative. Urinalysis had 3+ protein and 4+ blood without RBCs; urine albumin:creatinine ratio was 52.3 mg/mmol. Cardiac markers were elevated (troponin 17 137 ng/mL; CK > 7800 U/L).

A negative ASOT made rheumatic fever unlikely. Chest X-ray showed pulmonary edema and cardiomegaly; echocardiogram revealed dilated cardiomyopathy with EF 30–35% and normal valves. Abdominal CT demonstrated a distended bowel with splenic and renal infarcts. HRCT confirmed cardiomegaly with bi-basal atelectasis. Initial differentials included bacterial septic shock, vasculitis (antiphospholipid syndrome or medium-sized vessel vasculitis), and multisystem inflammatory syndrome.

He required intubation and increasing norepinephrine (0.7 μg/kg/min), meropenem, vancomycin, urgent dialysis, and cooling measures. An autoimmune panel showed low C3 (0.51 g/L) and C4 (0.04 g/L), and he received a low-dose steroid pulse (250 mg IV daily). Autoantibodies returned with a positive beta2-glycoprotein IgA antiphospholipid antibody and negative ANA, anti–dsDNA, ENA, pANCA, and cANCA. SARS-CoV-2 PCR from tracheal aspirate and nasal swab was negative.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 29-year-old Caucasian man with a history of hepatitis C, posttraumatic stress disorder, polysubstance abuse, and tobacco use was brought to the emergency department after being found agitated and erratically wandering the streets and then unresponsive with multiple skin abrasions. He reported ingestion and insufflation of “bath salts,” a history later confirmed by his family. He denied other medications or supplements and had no known drug allergies.

On examination, temperature was 107°F, blood pressure 91/52 mm Hg, and pulse 93/min. He was confused and intermittently agitated, with pupils 3 mm and equal. Cardiovascular exam showed weak peripheral pulses without jugular venous distention or murmurs; lungs were clear; abdomen was soft; no focal neurologic deficits.

Laboratory studies on admission showed features of severe rhabdomyolysis. Serologic testing confirmed chronic hepatitis C but was otherwise unremarkable. Serum toxicology tests were negative for ethanol, acetaminophen, and salicylates. Urine toxicology detected only lorazepam and cotinine but was negative for over 80 other substances, including cannabinoids, cocaine, ecstasy, ephedrine, lysergide, methamphetamine, methylphenidate, oxycodone, and phencyclidine.

Noncontrast CT of the head, MRI of the cervical spine, EEG, and chest and abdominal radiographs were normal. Right upper-quadrant ultrasonography revealed gallbladder calculi, a normal pancreatic duct, and an echogenic right kidney with prominent corticomedullary differentiation.

He received aggressive IV fluids, a norepinephrine infusion, and a bolus of amiodarone. Hyperkalemia was treated with sodium polystyrene sulfonate, calcium gluconate, insulin with glucose, and IV bicarbonate. For severe hyperthermia, he was given dantrolene and placed on cooling blankets. He was sedated, intubated, and mechanically ventilated, and received rasburicase for hyperuricemia. Urine output was 4200 mL over the first 24 hours, then declined to 825 mL and 150 mL over subsequent 24-hour periods. He was started on daily hemodialysis for volume control and solute clearance.

A 43-year-old man with no significant medical history presented in December with a 4-day history of fever to 38.8 °C, shaking chills, hemoptysis, and worsening dyspnea. He reported several months of intermittent night sweats, arthralgias of the wrists and ankles, and a 10-kg weight loss. One day before admission, he noted a painful ecchymotic lesion on his left calf; over the next 24 hours, similar lesions appeared on his abdomen, back, right upper arm, and right calf. His 3-year-old son had recently had a respiratory illness. On examination, temperature was 35.3 °C, blood pressure 117/75 mmHg, pulse 112 beats/min, respiratory rate 29 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 96% on room air. Bilateral wheezes were present, and there were multiple painful ecchymoses with hemorrhagic bullae over the trunk and extremities. Laboratory studies showed a WBC count of 9000/mm3 (87% neutrophils), hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, normal renal and liver function, lactate dehydrogenase 799 IU/L, erythrocyte sedimentation rate 81 mm/h, and C-reactive protein 38.5 mg/dL. Chest radiography and CT demonstrated multifocal alveolar infiltrates, and CT angiography showed no pulmonary embolism. Empiric intravenous ceftriaxone and oral azithromycin were started for presumed community-acquired pneumonia. On hospital day 2, a punch biopsy of a skin lesion revealed superficial and deep dermal thrombotic paucicellular vasculopathy involving skin appendages without significant neutrophils or leukocytoclasia. Tests for cryoglobulin, protein C, protein S, rheumatoid factor, anti–cyclic citrullinated peptide antibodies, anti–double-stranded DNA antibodies, complement levels, antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibodies, and anti–glomerular basement membrane antibodies were negative. Antinuclear antibody titer was 1:160; lupus anticoagulant was prolonged at 82 seconds (reference range, 27–41); anticardiolipin IgM was 64 (reference range, 0–12); and anti–phosphatidylserine IgM was >100 (reference range, <10). Nasopharyngeal testing for influenza antigen, streptococcal antigen, and Legionella antigen was negative. A FilmArray respiratory panel was positive for respiratory syncytial virus and negative for other respiratory viruses and atypical bacteria. Epstein-Barr virus DNA PCR was positive at 8696 copies/mL; tests for HIV, cytomegalovirus, and hepatitis A, B, and C were negative.

A 17-year-old nulliparous female presented with a two-year history of gradually progressive abdominal distension. She initially sought evaluation for bloating but was advised to diet for presumed weight gain. She denied pain, vaginal bleeding, or systemic symptoms. There was no personal or family history of cancer. On examination, her BMI was 20.5 kg/m2, blood pressure 125/85 mmHg, pulse 89/min, and SpO2 95% on room air. The abdomen was markedly distended with a palpable mass rising approximately 3 cm above the umbilicus. Transvaginal ultrasound demonstrated an 18 cm diameter ovarian tumor. Laboratory studies showed hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL with a microcytic profile (MCV 73.2 fL); APTT, INR, electrolytes, urea, and creatinine were normal. Tumor markers included HE4 69.1 pmol/L (N ≤ 60.5), LDH 202 U/L (N ≤ 48.5), with alpha-fetoprotein 4.54 ng/mL (N ≤ 5.8), CA-125 23.1 U/mL (N ≤ 35), and β-hCG <0.2 mIU/mL all within normal limits. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a large, fluid-filled lesion measuring 19.3 × 6.2 × 21 cm, located in the pelvis and mid-abdomen, displacing the uterus and compressing the aorta and inferior vena cava. The lesion appeared unilocular with a 1.5 mm wall and no septations or solid components, and was suggestive of an ovarian origin.

A 28-year-old woman presented with a 2-year history of hip pain following low-impact falls. Initial imaging revealed stress fractures of the left rib, left sacrum, and left femoral neck. Laboratory studies showed an elevated alkaline phosphatase level of 220 U/L (reference range, 30–95), a phosphorus level of 2.1 mg/dL (2.5–5.0), creatinine 0.56 mg/dL, and 25-OH vitamin D 14.8 ng/mL (30–95). Outpatient evaluation demonstrated 1,25[OH]2D3 <8 pg/mL (18–72), calcium 9.3 mg/dL, albumin 4.28 g/dL, parathyroid hormone 37.9 pg/mL, ferritin 16.9 ng/mL, 24-hour urine phosphorus 0.5 g (0.3–1.3 g), urine creatinine 0.9 g/24 h (1–2 g/24 h), thyroid-stimulating hormone 2.54 mIU/L, and fibroblast growth factor 23 (FGF23) 1241 RU/mL (<180). Bone densitometry showed Z-scores of −2.5 in the lumbar spine and −1.9 in the femoral neck, and an octreotide scan was negative. She was treated with calcitriol and phosphate and underwent percutaneous pinning of the femoral neck. She became pregnant; her phosphate and calcitriol were adjusted to maintain normal phosphorus levels, and genetic evaluation for hypophosphatemic disorders, including X-linked hypophosphatemia, was unremarkable. Family history was negative for bone disease. After a planned cesarean delivery, she continued to have disabling bilateral hip, knee, and ankle pain. On re-presentation, examination revealed a slow gait with a limp and lumbar tenderness. Current labs on calcitriol 0.5 mcg daily and elemental phosphorus 500 mg twice daily included alkaline phosphatase 204 U/L, phosphorus 1.6 mg/dL, 25-OH vitamin D 32 ng/mL, 1,25[OH]2D3 32.4 pg/mL, calcium 9 mg/dL, albumin 4.2 g/dL, and parathyroid hormone 74 pg/mL. Phosphate supplementation was increased to three times daily, raising the phosphorus level to 2.3 mg/dL. A gallium-68 DOTATATE PET/MRI showed a 9×8-mm intracortical lesion in the anterolateral right fibular head (standard uptake value [SUV], 65), with additional uptake in a right femoral neck stress fracture (SUV, 5.6) and bilateral calcaneal stress fractures (SUV, 4).

A 9-year-old boy presented with a 6-month history of swelling and moderate pain over the left clavicular area. He denied fever, weight loss, or trauma. He had received unspecified oral medications for one month at another center. His medical history was unremarkable, with no hospitalizations, chronic illnesses, or allergies. On examination, vital signs were normal. Musculoskeletal exam showed a tender 2 × 3 cm swelling over the left clavicle with a small clean overlying wound and erythema, without discharge. Shoulder range of motion was preserved, and other systems were unremarkable. Laboratory studies revealed an elevated erythrocyte sedimentation rate of 50 mm/h; complete blood count, renal and liver function tests were normal. Abdominal ultrasound was unremarkable. A chest radiograph demonstrated a midclavicular lytic expansile lesion with a minimally displaced pathologic fracture; the lung fields were clear.

raw.content:
A 57-year-old man with stage cS4a mantle cell lymphoma in complete remission after induction chemoimmunotherapy presented in August 2018 with painful swelling of the calves. There was no evidence of deep venous thrombosis or soft-tissue infection. He reported a brief gastroenteritis episode at that time. Diuretics gave transient relief, but over weeks the swelling spread to the upper extremities and trunk muscles. Systemic steroids and a short discontinuation of ibrutinib had no effect.

By November 2018, calf swelling worsened; examination was notable only for one slightly enlarged right inguinal lymph node. Laboratory tests showed elevated LDH and CK, with negative autoimmune serology. Analgesics provided minimal benefit. In January 2019, CT scan showed no lymphoma relapse but diffuse subcutaneous edema. The patient’s condition deteriorated, and he was hospitalized with generalized muscle pain, ECOG performance status 3, massive edema (especially of the lower extremities), and extreme muscle tenderness. Neurologic exam showed only weak symmetric fist closure and shoulder lift; no focal deficits.

Initial evaluations were consistent with myositis of unknown cause. Ibrutinib and rituximab were discontinued. Laboratory testing revealed elevated CRP, transaminases, CK, troponin I, myoglobin, and LDH, with reduced plasma protein, albumin, and IgG; leukocyte count was elevated. MRI of the thighs showed diffuse intramuscular and extramuscular edema. Muscle biopsy demonstrated interstitial and perivascular T-cell and macrophage infiltrates with variation in fiber size, centrally located nuclei, necrosis, and regeneration. The patient developed acute kidney injury secondary to rhabdomyolysis. Troponin I rose further; ECG revealed a new right bundle branch block and repolarization disturbances, and he developed atrial fibrillation. Cardiac MRI confirmed myocarditis. Over the next days, increasing somnolence and personality changes were noted. Brain MRI was unremarkable, but spinal MRI demonstrated a hyperintense lesion concerning for myelitis. CSF analysis showed leukocyte count 329/μl, lactate 3.5 mmol/L, and protein 79.6 mg/dl.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

vignette:
An 82-year-old man with epithelioid pleural mesothelioma (cT1N0M0) was treated with ipilimumab and nivolumab. After eight courses, follow-up chest CT showed new bilateral infiltrative shadows. He reported fever and dyspnea. Laboratory tests revealed elevated C-reactive protein and surfactant protein D levels; Krebs von den Lungen-6 was normal. Sputum cultures, procalcitonin, and SARS-CoV-2 PCR were negative. Serologic testing for anti–nuclear antigen, anti–aminoacyl–tRNA synthetase, anti-cyclic citrullinated peptide, anti-Sjögren’s-syndrome-related antigen A and B, and anti-neutrophil cytoplasmic antigen antibodies were all negative. He had no history of antigen exposure. Immunotherapy was discontinued. He received lascufloxacin and then tazobactam/ceftolozane without improvement; oxygen requirement increased to 2 L/min. Based on the clinical picture and imaging, grade 3 ICI-induced pneumonitis was suspected. He underwent methylprednisolone 1000 mg/day for 3 days followed by prednisolone 60 mg/day for 8 days, but chest radiographs remained unchanged and oxygen needs rose to 4 L/min. A second course of methylprednisolone 1000 mg/day for 3 days produced no clinical improvement. One week later, bronchoscopy showed no airway secretions. Bronchoalveolar lavage fluid contained 29% neutrophils, 58% lymphocytes, 13% macrophages, and a CD4/CD8 ratio of 0.33. Transbronchial lung biopsy showed no malignancy, and cultures of bronchoscopy specimens were negative. Based on these findings, he was diagnosed with steroid-refractory ICI-induced pneumonitis.

Giant Cell Arteritis primarily affects large arteries, typically in older adults, and does not align with the patient's symptoms.
Churg-Strauss Syndrome (Eosinophilic Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis) is associated with asthma, eosinophilia, and vasculitis, none of which are primary features in this case.
Rheumatoid Arthritis primarily affects joints symmetrically and does not explain the renal, serosal, and hematological findings seen in this patient.

Wegener's Granulomatosis (Granulomatosis with Polyangiitis) is a vasculitis affecting the respiratory tract and kidneys, but the specific serological markers and clinical presentation do not align with this diagnosis.

screen_response.screen_note: The vignette describes a patient with symptoms highly suggestive of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), including arthritis, serositis (pleural and pericardial effusions), renal involvement (proteinuria, hematuria, decreased GFR), hematological abnormalities (anemia, leukopenia, thrombocytosis), and positive serologies (ANA, anti-dsDNA, anti-Smith antibodies, low C3). The reference diagnosis is 'Type 4 renal tubular acidosis', which is a known renal manifestation of SLE, particularly in cases with lupus nephritis. Therefore, while SLE is a strong overarching diagnosis, the reference diagnosis is a specific complication/manifestation of SLE. The task is to evaluate the candidate diagnoses against the *reference diagnosis*, not the overall clinical picture.

vignette:
A 44-year-old Hispanic woman presented with six months of progressive generalized weakness, a 40-pound weight loss over four months, and two weeks of dyspnea. She had a five-year history of hypertension treated with lisinopril but had been noncompliant for over three years. She denied alcohol, illicit drug use, and was a lifelong non-smoker.

On examination, she appeared ill and wasted, with mucosal pallor and non-tender, rubbery axillary and inguinal lymphadenopathy. There was no skin rash, joint deformities, or peripheral edema. The abdomen was mildly distended but non-tender, without organomegaly. Respiratory examination revealed dullness to percussion and decreased breath sounds at the left lung base. Cardiovascular and neurological examinations were unremarkable.

Initial laboratory findings:
• Hemoglobin 6.6 g/dL, hematocrit 20.9%, platelets 544 ×10^9/L  
• White blood cell count 3.5 ×10^9/L (neutrophils 80.4%, lymphocytes 16%)  
• Sodium 131 mM/L, potassium 5.7 mM/L, chloride 105 mM/L, bicarbonate 18 mM/L  
• Blood urea nitrogen 60 mg/dL, creatinine 1.69 mg/dL  
• Urinalysis: trace proteinuria  

Chest radiography showed bilateral pleural effusions; thoracentesis revealed an exudative effusion. CT scans of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis and an axillary lymph node biopsy were negative for malignancy. HIV and tuberculin skin testing were negative.

On hospital day 4, she developed acute inflammatory arthritis of the elbows and knees. Serologic tests revealed high titers of ANA, anti–double-stranded DNA, and anti–Smith antibodies, with low complement C3 levels. Urinalysis showed pH 5, 16 WBCs and 27 RBCs per high-power field, and 24-hour urinary protein 0.81 g/day. Her estimated glomerular filtration rate was 53 mL/min/1.73 m^2, and leukopenia recurred on multiple occasions.

On day 5, she experienced worsening dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain. Repeat chest radiography demonstrated reaccumulation of pleural effusions, and echocardiography showed a pericardial effusion. Arterial blood gas and concurrent basic metabolic panel revealed a non–anion gap metabolic acidosis with hyperkalemia (pH 7.34, pCO2 26 mmHg, HCO3– 14 mM/L; Na 145 mM/L, K 5.5 mM/L, Cl 120 mM/L, HCO3– 19 mM/L, BUN 67 mg/dL, creatinine 1.09 mg/dL). Morning serum aldosterone was less than 1 ng/dL.

raw.content:
A 64-year-old woman presented with a slowly enlarging mass in the left labia majora over 10 years. Her vital signs were normal. On examination, the mass was firm, painless, immobile, and measured approximately 7 × 4 cm, extending toward the mons pubis. Routine laboratory tests were normal. 

Surgical history:
– In 2000, a mass in the Bartholin’s gland was excised; histopathology in 2007 showed chondroid syringoma.  
– One year later, a recurrence in the labia majora was resected; histology showed clear cell hidradenoma (“lobular glandular proliferation of cuboid cells with no anaplasia”).  
– Most recently, ultrasound revealed a 4.2 × 8 cm heterogeneous, hypervascular subcutaneous mass; CT scan demonstrated a 3.8 × 7.2 cm heterogeneous, contrast-enhancing lesion in the left labia majora extending to the anterior perineum, and a low-density focus in the liver suggestive of a simple cyst.  
– The vulvar mass was excised; on gross examination it measured 7 × 3 × 4 cm, was gray and well-circumscribed, and was reported again as chondroid syringoma.  

Three months later, the patient noted another recurrence near the fourchette. The lesion was excised and submitted for histopathologic evaluation.

raw.content:
A previously healthy young man presented during a month of religious fasting with a 1-week history of intractable vomiting, postprandial upper abdominal pain, and bloating. He had been compliant with fasting customs, was markedly lean, and reported progressive inability to tolerate oral intake. On examination, he was dehydrated and exhausted. After initial resuscitation, abdominal ultrasonography and plain radiographs showed marked gastric distension. A nasogastric tube was placed for decompression. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen revealed compression of the third portion of the duodenum between the superior mesenteric artery and the aorta at an acute angle. Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy was normal, with no intrinsic luminal lesions.

candidate_relations.reason: Cytochrome c oxidase deficiency is a specific mitochondrial disorder, but the vignette does not provide evidence for this specific enzyme deficiency. The normal lab results and MRI do not support this diagnosis.
Abdominal epilepsy is a type of autonomic seizure, which aligns with the reference diagnosis of 'Self-limited epilepsy with autonomic seizures'. The abdominal pain is a prominent feature.

Pancreatitis is an inflammation of the pancreas, typically associated with severe abdominal pain, elevated pancreatic enzymes, and imaging findings. The vignette describes neurological symptoms and normal lab results, making pancreatitis unlikely.

Acute intermittent porphyria is a metabolic disorder that can cause abdominal pain and neurological symptoms, but it is typically associated with specific biochemical abnormalities (e.g., elevated porphyrin precursors) not mentioned here. The normal lab results make this less likely.

MELAS syndrome (Mitochondrial Encephalomyopathy, Lactic Acidosis, and Stroke-like episodes) is a severe mitochondrial disorder. While it can cause neurological symptoms, the normal MRI and lack of lactic acidosis or stroke-like episodes in this self-limited presentation make it an unlikely fit.

Intra-abdominal shunt malfunction is a complication of shunts (e.g., for hydrocephalus) that can cause abdominal pain and neurological symptoms. However, there is no mention of a shunt in the patient's history.

Porphyria is a group of metabolic disorders that can cause abdominal pain and neurological symptoms. However, without specific lab findings (e.g., elevated porphyrins), it's a broad category and not specifically supported by the vignette's normal lab results.

Cyclic vomiting syndrome involves recurrent episodes of severe nausea and vomiting, which is present in the vignette. However, the prominent neurological symptoms (dysarthria, incoherent speech, confusion, disorientation) and the previous diagnosis of migraine, along with the overall presentation, point more strongly towards an epileptic or migrainous etiology rather than just cyclic vomiting.

Mitochondrial disorder is a broad category. While some mitochondrial disorders can present with similar symptoms, the vignette does not provide specific evidence (e.g., genetic testing, specific metabolic abnormalities) to confirm a mitochondrial disorder, and the reference diagnosis is more specific to epilepsy.

Migraine with abdominal aura is a plausible alternative diagnosis given the history of migraine and abdominal pain. However, the prominent and severe neurological symptoms (dysarthria, incoherent speech, confusion, disorientation, lack of eye contact) that occurred *during* the episode, without loss of consciousness, are more characteristic of an autonomic seizure than a typical migraine aura, especially given the reference diagnosis of epilepsy.

screen_response.screen_note: The case describes a complex presentation with abdominal pain, vomiting, and significant neurological symptoms that are self-limited. The reference diagnosis points to an epileptic etiology with autonomic features. Several candidates are plausible differential diagnoses, particularly migraine variants and other causes of episodic neurological/gastrointestinal symptoms.

vignette:
An 8‐year‐old boy with no significant past medical history presented with a 30-minute history of generalized abdominal pain followed by a single episode of vomiting. During the event he developed diaphoresis, mucocutaneous paleness, dizziness, dysarthria, incoherent speech, and lack of eye contact, without loss of consciousness, abnormal movements, or sphincter relaxation. The episode lasted 10 minutes, after which he reported a frontal headache (5/10) and persistent nausea. Family denied toxin or medication exposure. He had a similar episode 18 months earlier, diagnosed as migraine. There was no personal or family history of epilepsy or neurological disorders. Developmental milestones were age‐appropriate, and he was performing well in school.

On admission, his vital signs were normal except for blood pressure above the 95th percentile for age. Neurologic examination revealed confusion and disorientation; he could not recognize his mother or speak but could follow visual commands. Motor and sensory examinations were normal. Approximately 20 minutes after arrival, his consciousness and orientation improved. Over the next hours he had three additional self‐limited vomiting episodes and ongoing headache, which improved after a single IV dose of diclofenac (1 mg/kg).

Complete blood count, serum chemistries, and electrolytes (including sodium, chloride, potassium, magnesium, and phosphorus) were all within normal limits. Brain MRI with an epilepsy protocol was reported as normal for age.

raw.content:
A 25-year-old nulliparous woman presented with a 1-month history of insidious-onset right lower abdominal pain. She also had lifelong non-pitting edema of the left leg extending to the labia majora. She was otherwise healthy, with regular menses and no tobacco or alcohol use. On examination, she was afebrile, blood pressure was 110/80 mmHg, pulse 88 beats/min, respiratory rate 16 breaths/min, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. Cardiac and respiratory examinations were unremarkable. Neurologic exam was normal. Abdomen revealed a firm, non-tender, mobile mass measuring approximately 12 cm × 10 cm in the right lower quadrant; bimanual pelvic examination confirmed a right adnexal mass.  

Baseline hematologic, biochemical, thyroid, renal, and HIV/HBV/HCV serologies were within normal limits. Tumor markers were all in the reference range: carcinoembryonic antigen 1.14 ng/mL, lactate dehydrogenase 251 U/L, α-fetoprotein 2.16 ng/mL, CA-125 21 U/mL, and β-hCG 2.39 µIU/mL. Pap smear was negative.  

Transvaginal ultrasound showed multiple uterine fibroids and a large hypoechoic lesion in the right adnexa. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis revealed a well-marginated thin-walled solid-cystic lesion measuring 16.1 × 7.9 × 8.1 cm in the abdominopelvic region containing a 2.3 × 2.1 cm cystic component and a 5.8 × 5.7 cm solid component. A separate 7 × 3.2 × 2.8 cm cystic lesion was noted in the right parauterine region. Bilateral ovaries were not visualized separately. The uterus was bulky with multiple fibroids. Multiple small mesenteric lymph nodes were seen. Incidentally, a double inferior vena cava was identified, with the left cava draining via the left renal vein to the right-sided cava. Serology for filarial infection was negative.  

Although tumor markers were normal, the imaging findings were concerning for an ovarian neoplasm. A staging laparotomy with surgical excision was planned, with a provisional diagnosis of a malignant ovarian tumor in the setting of uterine fibroids and unilateral lymphedema.

candidate_relations.reason: AGEP is characterized by pustules, while the patient presents with vesicles and bullae. While both are severe cutaneous adverse reactions, they are distinct entities.

DRESS syndrome typically involves a morbilliform rash, eosinophilia, and internal organ involvement, which are present here, but the primary skin lesions (vesicles and bullae) and mucosal involvement are more characteristic of TEN. While there is overlap, the skin presentation points away from DRESS as the primary diagnosis.

Drug-induced liver injury is a manifestation of the patient's condition, but not the overarching diagnosis that explains the skin lesions and other systemic symptoms. It is a component of the broader drug reaction.

The patient's presentation with generalized painful fluid-filled skin lesions (vesicles and bullae), mucosal involvement (hemorrhagic lip crusts, penile erosion), and a history of ciprofloxacin use followed by rash and systemic symptoms (fever, liver injury) is highly consistent with Toxic Epidermal Necrolysis.

Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS) and TEN are on a spectrum, but TEN is characterized by more extensive epidermal detachment (>30% body surface area), which is implied by the 'generalized' nature of the vesicles and bullae. SJS is a less severe form of the same disease spectrum.
Wilson's disease is a genetic disorder of copper metabolism, which does not explain the acute onset of skin lesions, fever, and drug exposure.
Viral hepatitis would explain the liver injury and jaundice, but not the extensive skin lesions, mucosal involvement, or the clear temporal association with ciprofloxacin use.
Autoimmune hepatitis is a chronic liver disease and does not explain the acute onset of skin lesions, fever, and drug exposure.
Hemolytic-uremic syndrome is characterized by microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, thrombocytopenia, and acute kidney injury, which are not the primary features of this patient's presentation.
Erythema multiforme typically presents with target lesions and is generally less severe than the widespread bullous and erosive lesions seen in this patient, which are more characteristic of TEN.

screen_response.screen_note: The patient's presentation with widespread bullous lesions, mucosal involvement, and liver injury following ciprofloxacin use strongly points to a severe cutaneous adverse reaction, with TEN being the most fitting diagnosis given the severity and extent of skin involvement.

raw.content:
A 22-year-old man presented with a 15-day history of generalized painful fluid‐filled skin lesions, 7 days of yellow scleral discoloration, and 1 month of fever following removal of a tibial implant. Two years earlier, he had sustained a tibial fracture treated with internal fixation. After implant removal, he developed a surgical-site infection and persistent fever; he initially took paracetamol without relief, then obtained ciprofloxacin over the counter. Two days after starting ciprofloxacin, he developed generalized pruritus that progressed to fluid-filled rashes. He denied angioedema, dyspnea, abdominal distention, lower-limb swelling, hematemesis, melena, altered sensorium, alcohol use, or immunocompromise.

On examination, he was afebrile with stable vital signs. He had icterus but no pallor, clubbing, cyanosis, lymphadenopathy, or dehydration. Systemic examination was unremarkable. Dermatologic examination showed multiple generalized vesicles and bullae with non-hemorrhagic crusts over the trunk and extremities (palms and soles spared). Lesions were tender, with post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation. Mucosal findings included hemorrhagic lip crusts and penile erosion.

Laboratory studies revealed:  
• Leukocyte count 18,520/mm3 (neutrophils 64%, lymphocytes 22%, eosinophils 12%)  
• Hemoglobin 9.8 g/dL, platelets 423,000/mm3  
• AST 283 U/L, ALT 246 U/L, alkaline phosphatase 1390 U/L  
• Total bilirubin 14 mg/dL (conjugated 13.7 mg/dL)  
• Albumin 2.4 g/dL, INR 2.7  
• Renal function and electrolytes were within normal limits.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

A 48‐year‐old woman with a history of asthma presented with a 2‐day history of right lower‐extremity numbness and pain that worsened despite conservative measures. She denied any low back pain. On examination, manual muscle testing of the right tibialis anterior and extensor hallucis longus was 3/5, and gastrocnemius and flexor hallucis longus were 4/5; deep‐tendon reflexes were normal. Straight‐leg‐raising was positive at 70 degrees; the femoral‐nerve stretch test was negative. 

Plain radiographs showed degenerative scoliosis at L5–S1. Lumbar MRI demonstrated a right‐sided disc herniation at L5–S1 without significant nerve‐root or cord compression. Initial peroneal‐nerve conduction studies revealed a motor conduction velocity of 51.5 m/s. Ankle‐brachial indices were decreased (0.78 on the right, 0.73 on the left), but lower‐extremity arteriography showed no significant vascular lesions. Based on these findings, she was diagnosed with lumbar disc herniation and treated symptomatically with Neurotropin®. 

By day 7, muscle strength nearly normalized, but lateral leg pain persisted. On day 22, pain increased, and by day 26 she developed right foot drop (tibialis anterior, extensor hallucis longus, flexor hallucis longus, and peroneus longus 1/5; left side 4/5) with absent Achilles reflexes bilaterally. Urgent MRI showed no new nerve‐root compression. Repeat peroneal conduction studies failed to elicit an evoked myogenic potential. On day 30, she was unable to walk and was admitted for further evaluation.

vignette:
A 63-year-old woman was admitted with insidious upper abdominal pain unrelated to food ingestion and nausea, and after an episode of intense acute abdominal pain. She denied hematemesis or melena. Her medical history included untreated dyslipidemia and well-controlled hypertension on methyldopa. She was a smoker of ten cigarettes per day and had no family history of cancer. Physical examination was normal except for a palpable, movable mass in the upper abdomen. Laboratory tests, including a complete blood count, were normal without anemia. Conventional endoscopy revealed a large submucosal bulging mass in the posterior gastric wall with three Forrest III–type ulcerated areas; biopsy attempts failed to sample the submucosal mass, and ulcer biopsies showed only necrotic mucosa. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen demonstrated a well-defined, homogeneous, oval mass arising from the posterior gastric wall, measuring approximately 10×6×11 cm, compressing the second portion of the duodenum; the lesion had fat-tissue attenuation with central contrast enhancement and trabecular architecture but did not invade the peripheral layers.

vignette:
A 69-year-old woman presented with a several-month history of a painless, firm area of induration and mild erythema below her left lower eyelid. Her history included chronic scleritis treated successfully with NSAIDs, left levator resection for ptosis, and a dacryocystorhinostomy one month before the onset of the lesion. The mass persisted despite two courses of antibiotics for presumed postoperative cellulitis. Three months after surgery, the nodule remained stable in size. 

On examination, there was a focal, non-tender, indurated elevation along the inferior orbital rim. A CT scan of the orbits demonstrated soft-tissue thickening of the anterior-inferior orbital rim and lower eyelid without extension into surrounding structures or bony invasion. 

An excisional biopsy was performed. Intraoperative frozen sections revealed granulomatous inflammation. The final histopathology showed granulomatous inflammation with central necrobiosis, extensive Alcian-Blue positive mucin, and scattered multinucleated giant cells. There was no evidence of malignancy, and bacterial and fungal stains (Ziehl–Neelsen and Grocott) were negative.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

candidate_relations.reason: Granulomatosis with polyangiitis is a vasculitis, not primarily a granulomatous disease like sarcoidosis, although it can involve granulomas. The clinical presentation does not suggest vasculitis.

Idiopathic granulomatous gastritis is too narrow; the patient has granulomas in multiple GI sites (stomach, duodenum, ileum, colon, rectum) and elevated ACE, suggesting systemic sarcoidosis, not just isolated gastritis.
Whipple's disease is caused by Tropheryma whipplei, which was specifically tested for and found to be negative in this patient.
Gastrointestinal lymphoma is a malignancy, and while it can present with GI symptoms, the presence of non-caseating microgranulomas and elevated ACE points away from lymphoma.
Eosinophilic gastroenteritis is characterized by eosinophilic infiltration, not granulomas, and there is no mention of eosinophilia in the biopsy or blood work.

Crohn's disease is a chronic inflammatory bowel disease characterized by granulomas, but the widespread granulomas in the stomach, duodenum, ileum, colon, and rectum, along with elevated ACE and hepatosplenomegaly, are more indicative of systemic sarcoidosis than Crohn's disease, which typically has more focal GI involvement.

Blau syndrome is a rare genetic autoinflammatory disease with granulomas, but it typically presents in childhood with arthritis, rash, and uveitis, which are not described here. Sarcoidosis is a more common diagnosis for this adult presentation.

The patient presents with widespread non-caseating microgranulomas in multiple gastrointestinal sites (stomach, duodenum, terminal ileum, colon, rectum), hepatosplenomegaly, and an elevated angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) level, all highly characteristic features of sarcoidosis.
Ulcerative colitis is characterized by continuous inflammation of the colon without granulomas, which contradicts the biopsy findings of non-caseating microgranulomas throughout the GI tract.
Celiac disease is an autoimmune disorder triggered by gluten, characterized by villous atrophy, and anti-transglutaminase and anti-endomysial antibodies were negative, ruling it out.
Autoimmune enteropathy is a rare condition characterized by severe malabsorption and villous atrophy, not granulomas, and is typically associated with other autoimmune conditions.
Common variable immunodeficiency is characterized by recurrent infections and hypogammaglobulinemia, not primarily by widespread granulomas and elevated ACE levels as seen here.

screen_response.screen_note: The vignette strongly points to sarcoidosis with widespread non-caseating granulomas and elevated ACE. Crohn's disease is a plausible differential due to granulomas but less likely given the systemic nature and specific findings.

A 42-year-old man presented with a 1.5-year history of abdominal pain and three loose, watery stools daily. He had gastroesophageal reflux disease and hereditary hemochromatosis (grade 3 iron overload, mild portal fibrosis, C282Y homozygosity). He denied rectal bleeding, fever, or weight loss. Vital signs were normal, and physical examination was unremarkable. 
 
Laboratory evaluation showed negative ova and parasites, bacterial culture, fecal leukocytes, and Clostridium difficile NAAT. Histoplasma antigen, anti-transglutaminase, and anti-endomysial antibodies were negative. Rapid plasma reagin and Tropheryma whipplei testing were also negative. 
 
Colonoscopy revealed erythematous mucosa in the transverse colon and rectum and congestion in the terminal ileum. Esophagogastroduodenoscopy showed diffuse gastric erythema with erosions and duodenitis. Biopsies from the stomach, duodenum, terminal ileum, colon, and rectum all demonstrated non-caseating microgranulomas; acid-fast bacilli and fungal stains were negative, and no Helicobacter pylori organisms were identified. 
 
CT of the abdomen and pelvis showed hepatosplenomegaly; a prior liver biopsy showed no granulomas. Chest CT was unremarkable. Angiotensin-converting enzyme level was elevated at 77 U/L.

A 40-year-old previously healthy man was admitted after 1 week of progressive apathy, unresponsiveness, and immobility. He became bedridden and required a feeding tube and urinary catheter. On transfer, he was in a vegetative state.  
Vital signs: temperature 36.5 °C, heart rate 80 bpm, blood pressure 135/78 mmHg, Glasgow Coma Scale 7 (E3 V1 M3). Pupils 3.5 mm, briskly reactive; corneal reflexes present. Lumbar puncture: opening pressure 50 mmH₂O; CSF clear, protein 3.64 g/L, glucose 2.6 mmol/L (blood glucose 5.38 mmol/L), chloride 123 mmol/L, leukocytes 0/mm³. CSF India ink stain and bacterial cultures were negative. CSF oligoclonal bands, AQP4, MOG, and GFAP antibodies were negative; CSF fungal cultures were negative.  
Imaging: Brain CT showed a hypodense lesion in the corpus callosum. MRI revealed a homogeneous mass in the corpus callosum body, hypointense on T1, isointense on T2 FLAIR, with rim enhancement and surrounding vasogenic edema on postcontrast T1. DWI demonstrated rim hyperintensity but no central restricted diffusion.

raw.content:
A 36-year-old woman presented with persistent severe pain on the left side of her face. Two months earlier, on the day after receiving her third dose of the Pfizer-BioNTech COVID-19 vaccine, she experienced episodic sharp, electric-shock–like pain initially affecting the entire left hemiface. Within days, the pain localized to the V2 and V3 distributions of the left trigeminal nerve. Attacks lasted 4–5 seconds, were triggered by jaw movement during eating or tooth brushing, and reached 10/10 on a numeric pain scale. She reported allodynia to cold air and hypersensitivity to touch in the affected area. During attacks, she described distorted sensations in the V2 region, but sensory testing was otherwise normal. She had no other neurological deficits, no relevant past medical or family history, and prior doses of the same vaccine had been uneventful. Routine laboratory tests, including D-dimer, were normal. RT-qPCR for SARS-CoV-2 and other infections was negative. Contrast-enhanced MRI of the head showed no abnormalities.

raw.content:
An 87-year-old Cantonese-speaking man with Alzheimer’s dementia, hypertension, stroke, hyperlipidaemia, gout, peptic ulcer, and chronic kidney disease presented with one week of increasing left leg pain and weakness, impaired mobility, and a single episode of urinary incontinence. He also reported anorexia and a 12% body-weight loss over six months.  
On examination, his blood pressure was 88/45 mmHg (responsive to IV fluids), heart rate 96/min, temperature 36.4 °C, and oxygen saturation 95% on room air. He weighed 51 kg (BMI 19 kg/m2). Cardiac and chest examinations were unremarkable. Abdominal examination was normal. Neurologic examination showed 4/5 strength in left hip and knee flexors and extensors; the rest of the exam was normal.  
Initial laboratory results demonstrated elevated inflammatory markers (CRP 76 mg/L, WCC 11.9 × 10^9/L, neutrophils 8.5 × 10^9/L) and pre-renal acute-on-chronic kidney injury.  
An initial differential of cauda equina syndrome or epidural abscess prompted an urgent MRI of the lumbar spine, which showed mild foraminal narrowing at L5–S1 but no central canal stenosis or abscess. He was admitted for possible sepsis; chest X-ray, atypical pneumonia serology, and urine microscopy and culture were all unremarkable. A plain X-ray of the left hip showed no fracture.  
Despite analgesia, his left hip pain worsened, strength declined to 2/5 at the hip and 3/5 at the knee, and CRP and ESR continued to rise. A left hip ultrasound revealed a small anterior joint effusion. Normal tumour markers, MRI of the hip, and an isotope bone scan argued against malignancy. Attempts at hip aspiration were unsuccessful. Colchicine was started for presumed crystal arthropathy and atorvastatin was discontinued for possible myopathy, but creatine kinase was normal, and symptoms persisted.  
An MRI of the hips and pelvis then demonstrated bilateral iliacus and iliopsoas muscle oedema with enhancement and a left-sided insertional tendinopathy, with no evidence of trochanteric bursitis.

What is the most likely diagnosis?

raw.content:
A 60-year-old man with a history of heavy cigarette smoking, emphysema, hypertension, and prostate cancer in remission presented with a 4-hour history of acute right lower-quadrant abdominal pain. On admission, he was febrile (38.5°C), hypotensive (systolic blood pressure 90 mmHg), and tachycardic (heart rate 110/min); examination revealed peritonism in the right lower quadrant. Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen showed a perforated appendix with a 51×31×26 mm collection and surrounding fat stranding, innumerable hepatic nodules, mural thickening of the cecum and sigmoid colon, and marked mesenteric, para-aortic, and portocaval lymphadenopathy; there was also pulmonary consolidation and collapse in the right lower lobe. The patient underwent exploratory laparotomy, which revealed a perforated appendix with four-quadrant purulent contamination and a thickened, woody sigmoid colon; a subtotal colectomy with end ileostomy was performed. Postoperatively, he remained ventilated. On day 2, CT of the chest for staging demonstrated bulky multi-station mediastinal lymphadenopathy contiguous with soft tissue thickening enveloping the right lower and middle lobe bronchi. An extubation attempt on day 3 failed, and the patient died on day 6 after withdrawal of care.

raw.content:
A 21-year-old woman with autism spectrum disorder (on risperidone) and intellectual disability was brought to the hospital after a witnessed collapse. She had no prior history of syncope, cardiac arrest, or known cardiovascular disease, and her family denied any illicit drug or alcohol use. While at a noisy auto mechanic shop, she became pale and lost consciousness; bystander ECG showed ventricular fibrillation. Return of spontaneous circulation was achieved after two defibrillations. On arrival, her blood pressure was 93/70 mmHg, pulse 86 bpm, and oxygen saturation 100% (bag–valve–mask). An intravenous amiodarone infusion (1 mg/min) and oral amiodarone 400 mg were administered. On examination she was comatose (GCS 3), with agonal respirations; cardiovascular examination was unremarkable. In the intensive care unit, her differential diagnosis included channelopathies, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, and metabolic abnormalities. Laboratory tests showed normal chemistry panel and electrolytes. Initial electrocardiogram revealed sinus rhythm with interpolated premature ventricular complexes and a QTc of 380 ms, without any evidence of infarction, pre-excitation, or Brugada pattern. Transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated an ejection fraction of 45–50%, normal wall thickness, and no valvular abnormalities.

A 65-year-old man with benign prostatic hyperplasia presented for urologic evaluation. His prostate-specific antigen level was 0.796 ng/mL. Uroflowmetry revealed reduced urine flow, prolonged micturition time, and obstructive findings. He was started on oral Alfuzosin 10 mg once daily. On day 9 of therapy, he reported loss of appetite and malaise, followed by generalized pruritus, dark urine, and jaundice. He denied use of aspirin, acetaminophen, or herbal medicines and had no history of liver disease. On examination, he was jaundiced but had no stigmata of chronic liver disease. Laboratory studies showed leukocyte count 5.8 K/μL, AST 175 U/L (0–40), ALT 402 U/L (0–55), alkaline phosphatase 235 U/L (15–250), γ-glutamyl transferase 327 U/L (8–61), total bilirubin 7.6 mg/dL (0.2–1.2), and direct bilirubin 5.8 mg/dL (0–0.25). Abdominal ultrasonography showed normal liver, gallbladder, common bile duct, and intrahepatic bile ducts. Serologic tests for HBsAg, anti-HBc IgM, anti-HCV, anti-HAV IgM, anti-HEV, HEV RNA, and HCV RNA were negative. Autoimmune markers (ANA, AMA, ASMA, LKM-1) were negative. Metabolic evaluations—including transferrin saturation, ferritin, alpha-1 antitrypsin, ceruloplasmin, 24-hour urinary copper, and ophthalmologic exam for Kayser–Fleischer rings—were normal. Magnetic resonance cholangiopancreatography demonstrated a normal biliary anatomy.

A 35-year-old woman presented with an 8-month history of radicular pain radiating from her lower back down the left leg, with occasional tingling. The pain progressively worsened and was particularly severe by August. She denied any weakness, autonomic symptoms, history of trauma, or injury. On examination, she had mild hypesthesia in the left L5–S1 dermatome but normal muscle strength, normal abduction and adduction, and negative Lasègue, Kernig, Bragard, and Sicard signs. Electromyography showed neuropathic irritation of the left L4, L5, S1, and S2 roots, most severe at L5, with no denervation. Lumbosacral gadolinium-enhanced MRI revealed a solitary, completely cystic mass in the left L5–S1 foraminal zone extending along the course of the sciatic nerve into the left ischial groove, measuring approximately 13.9 cm in length and 1.9 cm in maximal diameter. The lesion was hypointense on T1-weighted images, hyperintense on T2-weighted images, and demonstrated peripheral rim enhancement, causing severe foraminal stenosis without attachment to pelvic organs. MR neurography confirmed that the mass arose from the sciatic nerve at the left ischial groove.

raw.content:
A 14-year-old girl presented with 2 months of progressive proximal muscle weakness. She initially noted difficulty combing her hair and rising from a chair; over weeks she became wheelchair-bound. She also reported morning stiffness of both small hand joints lasting about 30 minutes, dysphagia for solids and liquids, and poor appetite, without fever or weight loss.

Her medical history was notable for thyroiditis in 2015 that resolved without long-term therapy. Family history included a younger sister with Prader–Willi syndrome. She was up to date on vaccinations.

On examination, vital signs were normal. Neurologic testing showed symmetric muscle strength of 4/5 in the upper limbs and 3/5 in the lower limbs, with brisk reflexes more pronounced on the left. She could not stand from the wheelchair unaided. In the left hand, she was unable to make a fist or tuck the fingers; there was tenderness at the fourth and fifth proximal interphalangeal and metacarpophalangeal joints bilaterally. The remainder of the physical examination was unremarkable.

Laboratory studies revealed leukopenia (WBC 2.96 × 10^3/µL), microcytic anemia (hemoglobin 10.4 g/dL), elevated C-reactive protein (18.8 mg/L) and erythrocyte sedimentation rate (109.2 mm/hr), and normal creatine kinase (39 U/L). Thyroid function tests showed suppressed TSH (0.017 µIU/mL), elevated free T4 (20.9 pmol/L), normal free T3 (4.53 pmol/L), and markedly elevated anti-thyroglobulin antibodies (3410 IU/mL). Antinuclear antibody titer was 27 (reference <20); rheumatoid factor, anti-CCP, and ANCA were negative. Viral serologies, renal and liver tests, and other hormonal assays were normal.

Hyperkalemic paralysis was ruled out. Thyroid ultrasound demonstrated a multinodular goiter consistent with thyroiditis. MRI of the brain and lumbosacral spine was normal; cervical spine MRI showed a small C6–C7 disc herniation. Incidentally, the lumbosacral spine MRI revealed bilateral sacroiliitis. Dedicated MRI of the sacroiliac joints confirmed bilateral sacroiliitis; HLA-B27 was negative. MRI of the hips and pelvis showed bilateral thigh intramuscular edema with enhancement. Although myositis was suspected, electromyography and repeat creatine kinase were normal.

raw.content:
A 34‐year‐old African American man with hemophilia A, HIV‐1 infection, and hepatitis C virus infection presented with a 3‐month history of intermittent fever, unintentional weight loss, and progressive lip swelling with painful ulcerations. Six months earlier he had resumed antiretroviral therapy, with his CD4 count rising from 94 to 160 cells/mm3; the lip lesions developed approximately two months after the CD4 count began to improve. He had received multiple courses of antibiotics and systemic corticosteroids without benefit. He was taking acyclovir for herpes simplex prophylaxis and dapsone for Pneumocystis jiroveci prophylaxis. 

On examination, his lips were markedly edematous, with multiple superficial ulcers having heaped‐up margins. There was no hepatosplenomegaly. The initial differential diagnosis included herpetic ulcers, bacterial infection, fungal infection, and angioedema. 

Diagnostic studies showed an undetectable HIV viral load and undetectable hepatitis C viral load. A polymerase‐chain‐reaction assay for herpes simplex virus from an ulcer base was negative. Complement C1 esterase inhibitor levels were within normal limits. Gram stain, acid‐fast stain, and mucicarmine stain of lesion samples were negative. Fungal blood cultures and both urine and serum Histoplasma antigen tests were negative.

What is the most likely diagnosis?
